0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>More on the Airbnb and Uber share similar stories, and AI seems like a superb fit for framework migrations.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Are AI startups making the Gartner Magic Quadrant irrelevant?</span></strong><span> Gartner ranked AWS, Microsoft and IBM above Anthropic, Cursor and OpenAI in their “AI code modernization tools” ranking. This is most likely because the first three pay large sums of money to Gartner, but AI labs and vendors refuse to pay this “Gartner tax.”</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Industry Pulse.</span></strong><span> Another hours-long GitHub outage, GitHub alternatives are here and fighting for market share, Slack launches Slack Code, text generated by Claude to be watermarked, and Uber open sources SubmitQueue.</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>Before we start: apologies for the numerous typos last week. A reader asked for cute puppy pictures to accept my apology, and so I updated the post </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/4e94a1eb-ebc0-497f-94b3-27e2259e9dc7?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>with pictures of our 3-month old puppy.</span></a></em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>1. More on the “great engineering leader career break”</span></h2><div class="paywall-jump" data-component-name="PaywallToDOM" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;display: none;"></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Tuesday’s article about CTOs, VPEs, and senior engineering leaders taking extended career breaks seems to have hit a nerve, as I’ve gotten a lot of messages and comments on the topic from readers, making interesting points. Below is a selection of the feedback:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>The VPE role needs to adapt radically, and it’s important to be master of your destiny, </span></strong><span>says Roman:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“If the VPE is at least partially a master of their own and their org’s destiny, then they have to adapt their role in a radical way. There’s no middle ground; either you call upon your change management skills and succeed, or you continue doing whatever you did before AI and gradually become irrelevant.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There aren’t that many VPEs around, so I feel many of us are reinventing solutions to the same problems:</span></p></blockquote><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>How to retool our SDLC for a world where coding is not the long pole?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>How to make AI effective in monoliths and monorepos?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>How to balance human-in-the-loop and AI speed when operating in a brownfield or regulated sector?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>How to change a team’s culture and responsibility model when coding is no longer the core activity of most engineers?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>How to rethink the org model between horizontal and vertical teams due to AI disruption and the need to move fast?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>How to collaborate differently with PMs and UX who are more eager to deliver working prototypes?</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>How to prove the value of AI to non-technical executive management (and more importantly, to ourselves?)”</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Roman points out that Director+ folks are there for a reason: at that level you should get plenty of autonomy to carry out radical change.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>“Knowing I’m not alone makes me feel better.” </span></strong><span>I got a handful of messages from leaders who feel uncertain about what to do next because their role and the industry is changing, and there are no clear models about what works. We don’t even know what a sensible AI-native transformation looks like!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Exec retirements & semi-retirements seem to be increasing. </span></strong><span>A few readers messaged me to say engineering leaders at their orgs have retired the past six months, and one reader’s partner (also an engineering exec) semi-retired because the “job is not worth it anymore”.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>What about hope? </span></strong><span>Fellow author and friend Kent Beck enquired about the absence of a hopeful, tactical note to end Tuesday’s article with. Personally, I can say the article was an effort to capture and describe a strange, unfolding trend as it happens, and it didn’t cover every angle. Let me explain why this trend is unusual:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To become a senior engineering leader, a mix of tenure, good judgment, and interests in software and technology is needed. Being an engineering executive is not easy, but it’s impactful and important and, of course, financially rewarding. When things go wrong, these folks stay longer trying to fix things and often care a lot about their teams and the business. So, during a crisis, they are the ones who hang on longer than some ICs, for example. So, why are these leaders now leaving their jobs before colleagues like ICs do?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Also, I wanted to get the article out there without delay because several engineering leaders thought they were the only ones in this situation. One wrote that reading the piece was “like therapy.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>On potential tactical career moves to make, there wasn’t much else to report on Tuesday than what we included. So far, the only surefire thing that seems to work well for engineering leaders dealing with this change is to get AI-native experience.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The final part of that article featured practical advice from a former engineering manager at Cloudflare, who moved to Gitpod as VP of Engineering and helped the company turn “AI native” and eventually be acquired by OpenAI. Matt Boyle accelerated his career and successfully transitioned from middle manager to a thriving executive by taking a bet on the </span><em><span>right</span></em><span> company, after doing due diligence to ensure the founders there were serious about making drastic changes to ride the AI wave.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I talked with folks who moved jobs 6–12 months ago to places that are “winning” with AI, including one with a new manager who’s in “founder mode”. As also discussed in Tuesday’s article, it’s easier to manage “founder mode” at growing businesses when leaders can take on work the founder isn’t interested in.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>With so much change underway in software development due to AI, it’s clearly a hard time to be an engineering leader: tools are changing along with workflows, and so are roles and hierarchies as a result. In the best case, this requires reskilling and role changes at organizations, and it evidently also involves exits for some folks, and companies recruiting for new skillsets. In this scenario, it’s not possible to A/B test an approach! My tactical advice would be to also connect with peer CTOs and VPEs as sources of honest feedback and insights about what works.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/ded8b0bd-f806-49de-9745-76b37240eeb7?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Ebi Atawodi</span></a><span>, a Director of Product and a friend, told me about her personal “board of directors” of fellow professionals, from whom she gets advice on work and her career. If there was ever a time to have such a resource, it would be now.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>2. We need to talk about migrations with AI</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>OpenAI put an impressive-sounding case study about how they helped Asana save $5.9M with a single migration. From </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/09287fb3-3a8e-45a5-86ec-e8c8dc3f7530?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>OpenAI</span></a><span> (emphasis mine.)</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>“Asana cleared 5 years of engineering work in 2 weeks with Codex</span></strong><span>. Using OpenAI Codex, Asana replaced an outdated testing system in two weeks for about $12K.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For this project, Codex helped Asana’s engineers remove Enzyme, an outdated testing system that had made the company’s code harder to upgrade. Model and infrastructure costs came to about $12,000, compared with Asana’s roughly $6 million estimate for the previous staffing plan.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>After 1.5 weeks of engineering effort spread across two calendar weeks, Enzyme was fully removed. Model and infrastructure costs totaled about $12K. For comparison: the previous plan was expected to take at least five years and estimated to cost roughly $6M. The experience changed which long-running software projects the company believes are practical to take on.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For context, Asana migrated from Enzyme to React Testing Library, which indeed would not be a simple migration. However, their estimate of four engineers (each on circa $300K/year, according to OpenAI’s arithmetic), spending five years on the project, had me like:</span></p><div Source: </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/fd199353-f837-43b2-a03d-8a85e0484c41?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="text-decoration: underline;"><span>Airbnb</span></a></em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Airbnb’s team had to build loops to keep retrying migrations; once they did, 75% of files were migrated in just four hours, and the migrations were straightforward. They then built a more sophisticated refactor pipeline for the remaining 25% of tests; after building the pipeline, the new loop migrated most of the remaining tests (97%) in total, after running over 4 days. The remaining 3% was done with LLM input, with engineers finishing it in a week.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This was in March 2025, when the frontier coding model was Claude 3.7 Sonnet. Today, models are a lot more capable, such as the likes of GPT-5.6 Sol and Claude Fable 5.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>AI makes impractical migrations doable</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>On the basis that it took Airbnb six weeks, I find it credible that it took Asana two weeks to migrate what is probably a similarly complex test infrastructure from Enzyme to RTL, a year later.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>The time and $6M cost as quoted by OpenAI feels inflated. </span></strong><span>I assume the numbers were based on an estimate that a fulltime engineer could do a maximum of X tests migrated per day, where X was between 5 and 10. Then, calculate the number of engineering years this takes (perhaps 20 engineering years), and multiply by the cost of an engineer. You estimate a project like this when it’s an undesirable project you </span><em><span>really</span></em><span> don’t want to do as an engineer!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So, looking at it from this point of view: does it matter if the estimate was 1.5 years (Airbnb) or half a decade (Asana, hypothetically)? Or if the estimated cost was $1M or $5M? It would still be an </span><em><span>impractical</span></em><span> migration and a foolish endeavor: too long and distracting, at least, in the “traditional” way!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Pre-AI, years-long migrations were rare. </span></strong><span>In 2021, Sentry took 1.5 years to convert their frontend codebase from JavaScript to TypeScript. That was a migration of 1,100 files and 95,000 lines of code! Around 10 engineers worked on the migration, so if we assume a $300K-per-engineer cost, that’s a $2–4M cost for circa 95,000 lines of code.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Indeed, Asana’s reported $12,000 migration cost could actually cost even less if there was ruthless focus on cost optimization. </span></strong><span>What about using a model that’s 10x cheaper than OpenAI, like an open model running on inference providers? After all, why use the most expensive model, especially if a company already owns GPUs, running models, making inference practically free (except for power costs, that is.) For a first run, $12,000 would be affordable for a company paying $300K for engineers. But for subsequent runs, I’d wager it’s worth spending time optimizing the cost, and saving $10K per migration (or more!)</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Expect long-avoided migrations to finally happen</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A few months ago, Uber </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/945afe93-72f6-40fe-985f-164e959a3e32?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>shared</span></a><span> that they executed a massive JUnit migration in four months with two engineers and AI: moving 600,000 unit tests spanning 15 million lines of code (!!) by moving from the unsupported JUnit 4 to JUnit 5. During the migration, 1.25M lines of code were modified. This type of migration used to be impractical; with AI tools, it took eight engineering months of effort, plus AI costs.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And there’s the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/d0d1512b-5392-469d-98f8-ac84489f097a?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Bun migration</span></a><span> (530,000 lines of code from Zig to Rust in two weeks for a $165K API cost) as another example of drastically faster migrations with AI.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>The best part about rapid, AI-assisted migrations is not needing to worry about supporting “old” libraries. </span></strong><span>One of the main reasons library migrations have been such a pain was the need to keep supporting the old library or technology during the migration. Shortening this window could well be worth the additional cost, at least until we figure out how to drastically reduce the time and cost of these migrations, as well.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The shared characteristic of all of the above migrations is that engineers needed to plan for it, design verification loops, and be involved throughout. I always dreaded migrations, so I see it as good news that we have a new tool to use for “grunt work” like this.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>3. Are AI startups making the Gartner Magic Quadrant irrelevant?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Gartner has long been a “kingmaker” of software vendors with its ‘Gartner Magic Quadrant’ ranking. Vendors in the top right corner of this quadrant are marked as “leaders”. Enterprise decision-makers like CIOs and CEOs have traditionally paid a lot of attention to Gartner. But is it now sliding in relevance and becoming ‘legacy’?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There’s an issue that the reports Gartner produces on AI vendors seem increasingly detached from reality. href="https://substack.com/redirect/3eb00e21-b024-4634-a45c-94f166c32dcc?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>IBM</span></strong><span> with its ‘Bob’ product, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/c896613c-a04e-4ead-8001-30c561bf30c8?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>launched</span></a><span> in April this year. It’s the only tool in this bulletpoint list that can be tried out, and looks like a somewhat opinionated agent harness.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Rocket Software</span></strong><span>, which also </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a510836a-daa1-42d3-92db-5d7656d7c5d1?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>has</span></a><span> a “talk to an expert” message</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>BMC</span></strong><span>, a company whose </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/f7142c23-f749-4679-8b99-d8aebf41e414?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>product</span></a><span> is behind a “Get in touch” sign</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What AWS, Microsoft, Moderne, and IBM – the highest-ranked products in this list – share is that they’re customers of Gartner. I would suspect that Anthropic, Cursor, and OpenAI are not customers, and are absent from or lower-ranked by the quadrant.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Gartner has an effective business model:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Pay to access reports:</span></strong><span> the company charges anywhere from $10K to $50K per seat, per annum, to access in-depth reports and portals.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Pay to influence rankings</span></strong><span>: vendors can purchase “analyst hours” for $50K and up for access to a certain number of hours to spend on educating Gartner’s analysts about a product and answering their questions. These analysts write the Gartner reports.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Pay to share and distribute reports. </span></strong><span>Vendors ranking high on the list must pay Gartner for the right to distribute these reports. </span><em><span>This also means that if a vendor makes it to this list without paying, they will still need to get an expensive Gartner subscription to see what Gartner wrote – as I confirmed with a startup who made it on such a list, without paying, but was unable to read what it said.</span></em></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Lack of disclosure.</span></strong><span> Customers paying tens of thousands for industry insights don’t know which vendors are paying Gartner because this information is not disclosed.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s a booming business: Gartner generates $6B per year from a two-sided market that charges both customers and suppliers, and leading vendors have played along and paid the “Gartner tax” to be featured. But AI companies are not following suit; they don’t pay Gartner, so the reports are looking increasingly silly as Gartner cannot risk large customers like AWS, Microsoft or IBM not being designated as leaders in the reports.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Non-customers like Anthropic, OpenAI, and Cursor have objectively better products, and seem to be downranked or omitted from reports, which reduces the credibility of the research in my opinion. Why trust Gartner and pay for inaccurate information?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>A few years ago, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/42cea181-3047-4273-b20c-195afb67fa2b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>I went head-to-head</span></a><span> with Gartner on Cloud Development Environments vendors. Gartner’s $50K+ report covered 11 of them, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/42cea181-3047-4273-b20c-195afb67fa2b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>my deepdive</span></a><span> covered 28. At the time, feedback from Gartner subscribers was that my report was more ‘pragmatic’ than what a Gartner subscription unlocked.</span></em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>4. Industry Pulse</span></h2><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>GitHub’s eight-hour outage… again</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>GitHub’s poor reliability is an ongoing issue, </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/0aab4e94-4241-4b61-9428-22acfe05ec6b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>caused by</span></a><span> increased AI-related load (agents hitting GitHub’s services far more often). GitHub is prioritizing reliability but seems to be hitting large outages, over and again. This Monday, the service </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/860dd8db-27b9-42ec-b65b-bf6cd98e152c?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>was degraded</span></a><span> for eight hours, with 20-50% of requests failing across API, PRs, Actions, and Copilot.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To GitHub’s credit, they shared details a day later: the problem </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/860dd8db-27b9-42ec-b65b-bf6cd98e152c?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>was caused</span></a><span> by network saturation:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“The immediate cause of the failure was network saturation on load balancers in central US due to a new peak in traffic. Originally this was caused by an Istio sidecar pod reaching its concurrency limits and failing to auto scale correctly because of a misconfigured policy that watched host service but not sidecar limits. One failure cascaded to more and eventually four HAProxy nodes exhausted their flow limits, degrading the gateway auth path and causing widespread authentication latency and failures. The problem was worsened by optimistic retry logic which overloaded internal load balancers. Pausing HAProxy on those nodes simultaneously produced immediate broad recovery.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A few notes:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Sidecar</span></strong><span>: a Kubernetes pod usually runs multiple containers: an application container, and a sidecar container.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure Not too different from a sidecar bolted onto a Kubernetes container</figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The “sidecar” name comes from a motorcycle’s sidecar that’s bolted onto the side without changing the motorcycle any further. In software, sidecars usually provide services like logging, monitoring, security, and networking without modifying the application itself.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this outage, the sidecar (Istio) reached concurrency limits and failed at its job of scaling up the infrastructure.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>HAProxy</span></strong><span>: a reverse proxy and load balancer, routing TCP or HTTP traffic.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Exhausting the flow limit</span></strong><span>: all available TCP connection slots were occupied.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Optimistic retry logic: </span></strong><span>in the case of the network not responding, retries were made, assuming the service worked fine and that there must have been a network issue. But the services (proxies) were overloaded, which caused a retry storm!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/860dd8db-27b9-42ec-b65b-bf6cd98e152c?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>The full writeup</span></a><span> is interesting to read, as service traffic went up from ~8,000 requests per second (RPS) to ~80,000 RPS due to the retry storm. Even after finding the issue, dealing with this thundering herd problem took hours. </span><em><span>Thanks to the GitHub team for sharing the summary.</span></em></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>GitHub alternatives are here & fighting for market share</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>With convenient timing, Cursor </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/1595d1dd-1e51-4630-8c14-faeb237ff6e1?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>announced</span></a><span> its own GitHub competitor, Origin, during GitHub’s eight-hour outage. Unfortunately, Origin depends on GitHub, so the outage </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/eed13479-2310-4ffe-9f16-1149baff72b2?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>also impacted</span></a><span> Origin.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Origin joins </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7a6ac2a0-f545-4b89-a3d0-2a3c740193ea?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Entire</span></a><span> – cofounded by Thomas Dohmke, the last CEO of GitHub – as another “GitHub, but designed for AI load” product. Entire mirrors git repos globally to increase availability, and stores coding agent sessions and their contexts. I’ve been using it for a few weeks, and like how it works alongside my existing GitHub repos. </span><em><span>Disclaimer: I largely stopped angel investing in 2022, but </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/53ec56fe-48a9-4ea8-b7b6-97e7beb639d2?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>am an investor in Entire</span></a><span>. It’s my one-and-only angel investment of the last three years. See </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/53ec56fe-48a9-4ea8-b7b6-97e7beb639d2?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>all my investments.</span></a></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A day after the GitHub outage, Code.storage was also </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/9dfcb066-0c5d-4229-80c8-4df88b431242?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>announced</span></a><span> as being available.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Origin, Entire, and Code.storage have all realized the same opportunity: GitHub was not built with agents in mind, and nor for throughput or UX. So, these companies are building their own implementations of what they believe will be more reliable services for helping devs work more efficiently with AI coding agents.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Of course, GitHub surely won’t be giving up, but does seem to have its hands full solving its persistent reliability woes, and Slack seems set to be the place where non-engineers and engineers collaborate on software. It’s interesting that Slack faces zero competition from Teams or Discord in integrating AI coding agents. Who’d have thought Slack would be a big winner in AI coding? Not me!</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Text generated by Claude to be watermarked</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Claude models are to start generating watermarks embedded inside the text they generate, without any hidden characters or symbols. Here’s how it works, as </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/7c140ec6-7061-4882-b0f5-4405a9a652fd?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>explained by</span></a><span> Anthropic (emphasis mine):</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Large language models like Claude work by generating one word at a time. Each time the model decides on the next word, it chooses among a list of potential candidates, ultimately selecting the most sensible or likely based on the preceding text.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Take the sentence “The weather today was cold and…”. The next word is very unlikely to be “sugary.” But it is quite likely to be “overcast” or “grey.” Under most circumstances, it doesn’t matter much to the reader which of these latter two words the model ultimately chooses—the meaning of the sentence is largely the same either way. In cases like this, the choice is settled by a random number.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Watermarking uses low-stakes choices</span></strong><span> like these—which occur many times over a piece of generated text—</span><strong><span>to leave a pattern in Claude’s responses</span></strong><span>. That pattern is undetectable to the reader, but is detectable to anyone who has a key that encodes it.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Watermarking uses Google DeepMind’s </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/bc6d14c7-9466-43b1-8111-d485646dfa53?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>SynthID-Text approach</span></a><span>, and research shows that readers cannot differentiate between watermarked text and text without it. But why is Anthropic implementing watermarking?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The official reason is that the company </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e988c43a-15ab-4f95-980a-24370adaa57d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>signed</span></a><span> a commitment to comply with the EU AI regulation, which mandates watermarks be placed in AI-generated text. OpenAI also signed this commitment, so will also implement watermarking. Anthropic will apply watermarking globally.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I’d speculate that a secondary reason is that watermarking makes it a lot easier to detect AI output and exclude it from future training data. It’s interesting to remember that an LLM, deep down, is still a probability machine which can be watermarked to be detectably different from human writing! Also, I believe that watermarking will make it easier to reliably detect AI writing, so it’s worth keeping this in mind when producing written materials like blogs, case studies, and newsletters like this one. When it’s so easy to endlessly produce written content that’s generated by AI to be average in a very real statistical sense, there’s concrete value in words with the human touch which aren’t churned out by a robot.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>In this publication, we don’t have AI-generated text in any article, and employ AI in a limited capacity for deep research on topics we’re exploring. We use it as a spellcheck tool after we finish writing articles to confirm details such as company and individuals’ names, which both non-AI spellcheckers and humans equally struggle with.</span></em></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Uber open sources SubmitQueue</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>An impressive internal infrastructure component at Uber is SubmitQueue; a speculative merge queue that kept the mobile monorepo consistently green. It did this despite a mobile CI run taking 30-60 minutes to complete, and 100+ pull requests being merged in the monorepo, hourly. Last year, Uber published a paper on it titled </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/41b492f3-8cb2-42b2-bc6d-e892eef94eec?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>CI at Scale: Lean, Green, and Fast.</span></a></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><span>This interesting piece of technology </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2b724043-11c4-4191-a539-8bacd9063cd4?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>is now open source</span></a><span>. In the past, smaller and medium-sized companies would definitely not have needed such a system, but with AI agents committing more code a lot more often, it could be useful to have something like SubmitQueue in place to ensure the main branch stays green, and that code which breaks tests does not get pushed to production.</span></p></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;margin-bottom: 16px;overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: break-word;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em>This post is only for paying subscribers of </em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9uZXdzbGV0dGVyLnByYWdtYXRpY2VuZ2luZWVyLmNvbT91dG1fY2FtcGFpZ249ZW1haWwtaG9tZSZyPTM2eGwxbyIsInAiOjIxMjAzNzA4MCwicyI6NDU4NzA5LCJmIjpmYWxzZSwidSI6MTkzMDQzMTQ4LCJpYXQiOjE3ODcyNDg2NzksImV4cCI6MjEwMjgyNDY3OSwiaXNzIjoicHViLTAiLCJzdWIiOiJsaW5rLXJlZGlyZWN0In0.2htbVvrvLivtV_GajUgD1fIh4VAcYS79OnmcvnedTnM?" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">The Pragmatic Engineer</a><em>. 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;margin-bottom: 16px;overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: break-word;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><span>A schema change is usually one of the most difficult types of change for a software system. However, it might look quite small and simple in review. For example, it might be something as simple as a column being renamed, or a new field being added to a particular event, or a response payload dropping a field that was not being used.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To make matters more complicated, the migration goes smoothly and cleanly during the staging phase, but unrelated services and components start failing as soon as the change is deployed to production. On investigation, it is found that nothing was wrong with the migration itself. But it took effect while two versions of the application were still running against the same database, and only one of those versions referenced the modified schema.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This situation is common with schema-related changes. It is also not limited to the deployment window. For example, rows written years ago can get produced by application code that has since been replaced. The messages sitting in a queue were published before the current version of the consumer was written. Mobile app versions from eighteen months back are still installed on real devices and still calling the API. In each case, data written under a particular schema version is read under a different version, resulting in multiple issues.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this article, we will look at schema evolution and strategies for the same. Here’s what we will cover:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Why more than one schema version is always in play at the same time</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 In this episode, I sit down with Addy and we talk about his path from building a web browser aged just 16 to becoming a director at Google. We discuss what he learned from building tools for millions of developers, Google’s engineering culture, and why he continued doing hands-on coding work as a manager. We also get into how he works with AI agents today, the risks of ‘cognitive surrender,’ his approach to ‘loop engineering,’ and why it’s good to develop skills in product management, go-to-market, and other areas.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><strong>Takeaways from the conversation with Addy</strong></h3><a class="youtube-wrap" href="https://substack.com/redirect/6561fa3b-c8ce-40c2-aad2-79da84630f38?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" target="_blank" data-component-name="Youtube2ToDOMStatic" style="display: block;margin: 32px 0;"><img src="https://substackcdn.com/image/youtube/w_728,c_limit/l_youtube_play_qyqt8q,w_120/2fyPnxKu8ZM" style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;max-width: 100%;height: auto;margin: 0 auto;display: block;width: 100%;"></a><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Here are eleven interesting points from the chat with Addy:</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>1. Addy built a web browser from scratch, aged just 16. </span></strong><span>Back then, a pain point was that Addy had to carry floppy disks to his local library to download data. To speed up browsing, he built a browser that opened multiple connections when fetching webpages.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>2. Publishing free educational materials helped Addy land a job at Google. </span></strong><span>A documentary about Google which he watched as a youngster made Addy want to work somewhere like it. Later, Google noticed his work in publishing educational resources about frontend and JavaScript development. The company reached out about a DevRel-and-builder role, and Addy was hired to join the Chrome team.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>3. Chrome DevTools was an effort by Google to meet web developers in the browser</span></strong><span>. Today, DevTools is one of the closest things Google has to an IDE (not counting Antigravity, that is), but the project started as a way to add tools to the browser to help debug web applications. As web engineers started to use more complex frameworks and build chains, DevTools added capabilities like source-map-aware debugging, hiding library code, mobile device emulation, tooling for service workers, and more.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>4. Most developers don’t understand memory management. </span></strong><span>Addy says this is because memory debugging tooling has not advanced in a decade, and remains a hard problem to solve. This is despite making improvements in runtime performance debugging in Chrome DevTools (</span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e4ccf87e-6b77-4b63-ab9e-a6a7b21fd82d?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>flame graphs</span></a><span> and </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a824bfa2-c802-4f00-a49b-2fb4c1984092?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>deep tracing</span></a><span>).</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>5. Becoming accountable on a weekly basis for a top company goal is the biggest difference in a director of engineering at a major tech company.</span></strong><span> Addy worked his way up from engineer to Director of Engineering at Google, and I asked what the biggest change was when he made it to that level. Being on the hook and reporting regularly on a top company goal was something he found entirely new, Addy said.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>6. A big culture shift at Google in the last two years has been VPs and SVPs coding on weekends. </span></strong><span>Naturally, this is because AI tools make coding much easier. During his last two years at Google, it was common for these folks to talk about their weekend side projects and tools they used to build them.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>7. A big risk of AI-assisted development is cognitive surrender. </span></strong><span>Addy defines cognitive surrender as the erosion of your comprehension of the problems being worked on, and of your own memory of what’s going on. He recommends pushing back against this by understanding every major decision an LLM makes. Unfortunately, his former method of reading the AI’s </span><em><span>entire</span></em><span> reasoning process is no longer practical given how much output agents can generate, but you’ll still want to understand the most important decisions.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>8. Aim for mutual amplification when using AI tools. </span></strong><span>The aim is to do two things simultaneously:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Help the agent improve throughout the task by having it log its decisions and key learnings</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>You also improve by reviewing, understanding, and internalizing what the agent does and how you can learn from it</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>9. Addy believes software engineers will always be important because an AI model cannot be accountable. </span></strong><span>Accountability for code and software is possible even if the accountable party didn’t write the code, as is the case in projects like Chromium, where designated engineers own parts of the codebase. They’re responsible for approving and rejecting contributions, and for shaping that part of the codebase. Addy reckons that a “what am I accountable for?” mindset will be adopted by many software engineers.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>10. Addy is bullish about software engineering’s outlook. </span></strong><span>Every time the profession has made it easier to create software, we’ve created exponentially more software. Addy predicts the same will happen with AI, and that the total addressable market of people building software will get much bigger.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>11. Advice on where to invest efforts as engineers in the coming years.</span></strong><span> In his words:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“What we are very likely to see happen next with engineering careers (as well as product and other roles) is the unbundling of them, so that an engineer also has product sense, while a product person also has engineering sense, or UX sense.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>[You should] think about the non-engineering things if you don’t [usually] have the time to think about product or technical evangelism, or go-to-market approaches, or any other parts of how businesses are successful.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>If you can show employers that you are not just a builder, but someone that can help them as roles start to become a little bit fuzzier, then I think that you can be successful in these times. </span><strong><span>Don’t be </span></strong><em><strong><span>just</span></strong></em><strong><span> an engineer.”</span></strong></p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Retrieval Basics</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Standard RAG (Retrieval Augmented Generation) depends on a compact pipeline.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We take a collection of documents, slice each one into chunks of a few hundred to a few thousand tokens, and pass every chunk through an embedding model. The embedding model returns a vector, which is basically a long list of numbers standing in for the meaning of that text. Chunks with related meanings produce vectors that sit close together in the same numeric space. All of those vectors go into a vector index.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>At query time, the same treatment applies to the question. The question also becomes a vector, the index returns the handful of chunk vectors closest to it, and the original text of those chunks gets placed into the prompt alongside the question. The language model then generates an answer from the supplied text.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure rests on one simple assumption, which is that text answering a question would resemble that question. For a large share of queries, this assumption holds up well. For example, a question like “Which service owns the payments retry logic” contains the same vocabulary as the architecture decision record where that ownership was recorded. The vectors land near each other, retrieval returns the right document, and the citation points somewhere a reader can actually verify.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Similarity Limits</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This assumption about questions being similar to the answers holds for a specific class of questions, but it is by no means a universal thing.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Microsoft’s GraphRAG documentation distinguishes local queries from global queries. A local query has an answer that resembles the query and lives inside a small number of text regions, which covers most who, what, when, and where questions. A global query requires reasoning across large portions of a dataset, or across all of it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Our two example questions from earlier land on opposite sides of that line. The question “Which service owns the retry logic” is local. However, the question “Which failure causes recur most often across all postmortems” is global.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: answer for the second one goes down in quality is that the phrase “recur most often” produces a vector, and the index returns whatever appears nearest to it. Across a corpus of incident reports, the nearest neighbours will be documents using words like recurring or frequent, which is a coincidence of vocabulary. However, the real answer to the question exists across two hundred documents as a distribution, which spans the corpus rather than occupying one retrievable location.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A reasonable objection at this point is that modern context windows are large enough to sidestep the problem entirely. Microsoft tested exactly that, comparing GraphRAG against vector retrieval pulling in 8,000 and then 64,000 tokens of context. However, on global questions, the larger window left the gap open on comprehensiveness, diversity, and quality of supporting source material.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This outcome is usually labelled as a hallucination problem. What actually happens is that retrieval returns material with little bearing on the question, and the model produces fluent text from it.</span></p><div style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><hr relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Knowledge Graphs</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Crossing this boundary in terms of the quality of answers requires recording how documents relate to one another, instead of treating each chunk as an independent unit of text. A knowledge graph is one way to record it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A knowledge graph stores two kinds of things:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Entities are the nouns a corpus talks about, such as people, services, teams, incidents, and decisions.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Relationships are the typed connections between those entities.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Both carry a plain-text description.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Take one sentence from an incident postmortem: “The checkout service began returning timeouts after the payments team deployed the new retry handler on March 3.” Extraction over that sentence produces entities for the checkout service, the payments team, and the retry handler, along with relationships recording that the team deployed the handler and that the deployment preceded the timeouts.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Once thousands of sentences have each contributed nodes and edges, paths appear that no single document contains. An engineer may be namednamed in one design doc, a service is named in a second, an incident is described in a third, and the path from that engineer to that incident runs through both intermediate nodes.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>LinkedIn’s customer service team published results from this approach at SIGIR in 2024. Their support tickets had been stored as plain text, which discarded the internal structure of each ticket along with the connections between tickets. Rebuilding retrieval around a knowledge graph that preserved both improved mean reciprocal rank by 77.6 percent, and median per-issue resolution time dropped 28.6 percent in production. Similarly, Neo4j’s documentation separates the lexical graph, which links documents to their chunks, from the entity graph, which links the things those documents describe.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Most GraphRAG systems build both and query across them.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Graph Construction</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Building that graph from raw documents is a pipeline, and most of its cost concentrates in a single stage.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For reference, Microsoft’s documented indexing workflow runs through six phases:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Documents are sliced into text units, the same chunking step standard RAG performs.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A language model processes each text unit and extracts entities carrying a title, type, and description, along with relationships carrying a source, target, and description.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Entities sharing a title and type are merged across text units, and their descriptions collect into an array. A second language model pass compresses each array into one description. Relationships receive the same treatment.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Claim extraction runs optionally, producing time-bound factual statements about entities.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The assembled entity graph is clustered into a community hierarchy.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Community reports are generated, and text units, entity descriptions, and report contents are embedded into a vector store.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The merge step accounts for a lot of the expense. For example, a service mentioned across two hundred documents produces two hundred separate descriptions during extraction. Every one of those has to be reconciled into a single coherent description before the graph becomes usable.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Every extracted entity, relationship, and claim retains a pointer back to the text unit it came from. This pointer is what allows a generated answer to cite a specific paragraph in a specific document.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" model passes over an entire corpus add a substantial amount of inference. Microsoft’s documentation estimates graph extraction at roughly 75 percent of total indexing cost. Lastly, extraction quality also depends on prompts tuned to the domain.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As a separate point, FastGraphRAG replaces the language model in extraction with traditional NLP, treating noun phrases as entities and co-occurrence within a chunk as a relationship. Indexing becomes far cheaper, and the resulting graph carries considerably more noise</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Community Detection</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A graph of entities and relationships answers connection questions well. However, answering whole-collection questions requires one more layer on top of it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>GraphRAG runs hierarchical Leiden clustering across the entity graph. The algorithm recursively partitions the graph into clusters, called communities, and keeps subdividing until communities fall below a size threshold. The output is a hierarchy with several levels.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>These levels behave like a resolution control over the same underlying graph. Level 0 contains a small number of broad communities, each covering a large region. Deeper levels contain many more communities, each covering a narrower region. A single payments community at level 0 might split into separate communities for retry behaviour, settlement, and fraud checks two levels further down.</span></p><div style="border: none !important;vertical-align: middle;display: block;-ms-interpolation-mode: bicubic;height: auto;margin-bottom: 0;width: auto !important;max-width: 100% !important;margin: 0 auto;"></a></td><td style="text-align: center;"></td></tr></tbody></table></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For every community at every level, a language model generates a community report. Each report contains an overview of that community along with its key entities, relationships, and claims. Reports are then summarized again into shorthand versions for compact use at query time.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This is the step that makes whole-collection questions answerable. A summary of what a cluster of documents collectively says gets written during indexing, well before anyone asks about it. When a global question arrives, the material required to answer it already exists as text.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Which particular level supplies the reports is a decision with real consequences. Microsoft’s documentation states that response quality is heavily influenced by that choice. Lower levels produce more thorough answers because their reports carry more detail, but they also cost more time and more tokens because there are many more reports to process.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Query Modes</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>With a graph and a hierarchy of reports sitting on disk, retrieval can follow two structurally different paths. GraphRAG supports both.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Local search begins by matching the query against entity description embeddings, which produces a set of entry-point entities. From each entry point, expansion proceeds along five directions in parallel:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Text units that mention the entity.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Community reports that contain it.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Neighbouring entities connected to it.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The relationships forming those connections.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Covariates, meaning any extracted claims attached to it.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Each of those candidate sets is ranked and filtered independently. The survivors are packed into a single context window of predefined size. The expansion is bounded, and the ranking is explicit, which makes local search closer to a structured gather-and-rank operation than to open-ended pathfinding across the graph.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Global search leaves the entity graph untouched. Community reports from a chosen hierarchy level are split into batches, and those batches are shuffled so that batch ordering stays randomized. A map stage runs each batch through a language model and produces an intermediate answer where every point carries a numerical importance rating. A reduce stage then collects the highest-rated points across all batches and generates the final answer from them.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The mapping back to our payments questions can be made clearer now. The question: “Which service owns the retry logic” names an entity, so local search locates it and expands around it. Also, the question “Which failure causes recur most often” names no entity in particular, so global search aggregates across pre-written reports covering the whole corpus.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>See the diagram below:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic"
