20px;font-weight: 400;letter-spacing: -.15px;margin-top: 8px;width: 70%;padding-left: 15%;padding-right: 15%;text-align: center;"><em><span>Typical development process at Optiver</span></em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Significant changes start with a design review; a meeting at which a team presents their proposed changes to senior leaders whose job is to ensure the team did their homework: did they take into consideration all the relevant options and aspects of the problem?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>The teams still fully own the architectural decision making;</span></strong><span> this process is less about control and more about sharing knowledge and making informed trade-offs. Design reviews are time-consuming, so are not triggered for every change. Only those with the most impact on the architecture are reviewed.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Testing culture: pyramidal and “pre-AI”</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The expectation for everyone to push changes fast and the reality of a fairly fresh workforce means the potential exists for mistakes with disastrous financial consequences. That’s where a rock-solid testing infrastructure comes in.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Bugs are risks with no associated reward. </span></strong><span>Optiver’s automated test suite covers the whole range of the </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e5bdb23b-1368-4513-8f8c-97d0a63cf8da?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>testing pyramid</span></a><span>: unit tests, automated application-level tests, end-to-end regression tests. These are built to catch functional bugs and performance regressions with backtesting and simulation tooling.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Investment was made in this before AI, and has been paying big dividends during the age of AI. Non-engineering team members such as traders and researchers regularly push code to production without having to hand over work to engineers, confident that things will work in production.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Monitoring & incident detection</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>In contrast to risk management and testing, monitoring wasn’t always top-of-mind at Optiver.</span></strong><span> Teams historically prioritized shipping changes to production over adding relevant monitoring and alerting to the system. The team was much smaller and the overall system simpler, so keeping tabs on overall performance was easier.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But as the team and overall scope has grown, it started becoming increasingly tricky to sustain nanosecond-level latencies across production with hundreds of engineers pushing production changes daily. That’s why the company has invested heavily in monitoring over the past decade.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The performance ranges that apps operate in production are incredibly tight. Their monitoring is sensitive enough to detect a change in latencies introduced by a longer-than-necessary cable. This was a real production incident!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>At such latency levels, it’s sometimes hard to distinguish signal from noise. Some changes have a performance impact that’s close to </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/e2f28684-09c5-4860-8ee4-23394539f6d8?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>stochastic noise</span></a><span>, so it can take a couple of days of monitoring to tell if a result is statistically significant.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Since they’re able to attach direct profit/loss impact to each incident, most incident prioritization decisions are based on monetary impact. While many small, inconsequential incidents get logged, incidents with a meaningful impact are very rare – maybe a few a year – and their impact is very limited. This is a remarkable level of performance, given that the company makes tens of millions of trades a day and the trading income exceeds $4.5 billion.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Optiver gives teams full ownership and aligns their incentives, so they move at speed, with risk controls, testing, and monitoring tooling. With AI, the system comes under additional pressure, as more changes are flowing than ever at increasing speeds.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Risk management</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Risk is a key platform functionality at Optiver, and trading applications and services are enveloped by the risk management system, which monitors all apps’ signals and outputs (trade orders), and checks for unexpected behaviors. When an app is deemed to misbehave, risk management can decide to kill it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For use cases that are less latency sensitive, active trader oversight can also be involved: traders can stop apps, and tweak their system parameters based on observed performance. For latency-sensitive use cases, trading activity is automatically monitored post-trade to avoid adding latency on the hot path, and trading apps deemed to be misbehaving can be stopped.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Making risks visible and ensuring teams know how to react</span></strong><span> is woven in from building to running trading software:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Engineering culture:</span></strong><span> Systems are designed with risk in mind from day one, via knowledge sharing and design review sessions.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Robust testing and monitoring infrastructure: </span></strong><span>ensures risks are identified as soon as possible during the software development process</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Central risk platform: </span></strong><span>In a decentralized, federated team model, a central risk platform ensures a team has the “big picture” of the system’s behavior, and can react when needed.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>These multiple layers of protection are Optiver’s version of a well-understood </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/cdf77efe-78ed-4945-b9d1-b93019eaa93b?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Swiss Cheese model</span></a><span>, with each layer focusing on one cause of problems, and all the layers together covering the full problem surface area.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>7. AI at Optiver</span></h2><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Inflection point</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The engineering team at Optiver has used AI-assisted coding heavily – and Cursor in particular – since the early days of the technology. After the arrival of Claude Code with Opus 4.5 in late 2025, and stronger agentic capabilities, adoption took off at the prop shop.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>At that point, it was no longer a case of engineers playing around with cutting-edge tooling. David Gross, tech lead on the Options trading team, was inspired to look into agentic coding more deeply by a London trader who spun up multiple agents concurrently to automate work.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Future of agentic coding</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Optiver’s tech leadership doesn’t see AI coding as only a way of being more efficient. It’s also about rethinking how software is built, which changes how teams work together on building and shipping software. For example, David conceives an autonomous agentic coding loop in terms of an optimization problem with three axes:</span></p><ol style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Intent</span></strong><span>: defines the optimization objective, including documentation and architectural principles feeding into the prompt</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Back pressure:</span></strong><span> constrains the solution space via tests, code reviews, and making sure a solution is correct</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Velocity: </span></strong><span>limits how quickly an agent can iterate. More generally, how long does it take to find out if a generated solution works?</span></p></li></ol><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Any improvement to one of the axes represents a compounding investment because future AI-coding sessions will reuse it. Optiver’s leadership believes that convincing teams to improve the three axes is critical, as it builds the foundation of a future development platform. A big challenge here is that it’s “meta work” about redefining the work itself at a place where the primary focus is making profitable trades.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Adoption</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>At the time of publication, AI-coding adoption and investment isn’t universal at Optiver in the three axes, </span></strong><span>despite AI-coding tools being generally reasonably well adopted by teams and supported by the Platform team. This is a tension between short-term incentives and longer-term investment in a fully agentic coding platform.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Improving them requires time away from day-to-day projects, but a big part of engineers’ compensation is tied to trading profits (day-to-day projects), meaning teams are invested in a very literal sense, so must choose wisely between slowing down and investing in AI workflows, or maintaining business-as-usual and protecting their comp.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Meanwhile, senior management sees a fully agentic coding ecosystem as an unmissable opportunity: if they don’t take it, the company will pay the price commercially when competitors do.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Optiver’s culture of owning trading problems end-to-end necessarily limits AI adoption – and perhaps that’s a good thing. </span></strong><span>It’s refreshing to see a company not madly rushing to adopt a new technology just because everyone else is. If Optiver’s leadership believes that faster AI adoption is critical, it’ll be necessary to resolve the friction of engineers focusing on business outcomes, and being highly pragmatic about adopting AI tools that improve them.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>AI tooling stack</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To support teams improving their solutions along the three axes, the platform team has standardized key components:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Model gateway</span></strong><span>, giving everyone centralized access and cost control.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Agent + MCP platform</span></strong><span>. Teams quickly started building their own MCPs around services they wanted agents to utilize most. To avoid running them on their own desktops, the Platform team provides a centralized place to host MCP servers and agents. Some were common across many teams, so the platform team made them part of the platform offering.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/38e2fed3-5d8c-441e-91ed-29c5597b6052?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>LangSmith</span></a></strong><span> is included in the platform, providing teams with observability and evals of agents.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>These basic building blocks, on top of which teams build their own agents, enable the platform team to keep costs under control, which is becoming important due to AI token costs.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>How does this look in practice?</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Optiver has AI agents running in production with a major caveat: </span><strong><span>AI agents are only allowed to do a small subset of operations within their production area.</span></strong><span> Why? It’s all about risk.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Optiver’s platform teams provide guidance to teams via </span><strong><span>AI use cases,</span></strong><span> of which there’s a detailed taxonomy, and also a list of </span><strong><span>restrictions</span></strong><span> specifying what agents can and can’t do.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It seems to work. At Optiver, more non-engineers ship to production than before, but without production incidents which cause negative financial impacts. They say it’s because their longstanding focus on automated testing has proven valuable in the era of AI: every production change goes through thorough testing, where mistakes are usually caught.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>AI seems to be accelerating the “researcher-to-engineer-to-production” pipeline. </span></strong><span>In the past, it took a researcher/trader, plus an engineer working together to get strategies into production. Today, partly thanks to AI, traders and researchers ship strategy implementation to production by themselves.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>8. Hiring, career development & culture</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Engineers account for roughly 40% of the circa 2,200 workforce at Optiver. This might seem a fairly low percentage given algorithmic trading is the entirety of what they do, but there’s a fluidity between roles which means non-engineering folks also contribute to the trading system.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Europe was always Optiver’s center of gravity, but the company has been investing heavily in the US in recent years, and the tech team there has more than doubled in the last four years. Many teams are located across multiple locations to align with exchanges’ opening hours.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Business Acumen</span></strong><span>: expectations of business understanding</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Responsibility / Autonomy</span></strong><span>: expectations of independent working</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Depth / Sphere of Impact:</span></strong><span> expectations of wide-ranging work</span></p></li></ul><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>The original strategy: “hire 22-year-olds”</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In the early years, Optiver’s hiring strategy was to focus on new grads and growing them into specific quant-dev roles, Alex Itkin told us: “We built a multi-billion dollar company doing nothing but hiring 22-year-olds.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Core technical competencies are critical for job candidates to possess, but plenty of roles at Optiver need skills that are not taught at universities. The business has always looked to hire candidates who, given a problem, are able to work through potential options and trade-offs before getting to implementation.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The best predictor of long-term career success at Optiver, according to David, is not actually core technical skill. Actually, it’s having the personal drive to solve problems and get things done, and flexibility in the face of adversity.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Today: hiring experienced engineers</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As the company and its overall scope have grown, Optiver has hired more experienced engineers. Today, the company hires experienced engineers at a similar rate to Big Tech and other trading firms.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Hiring competition</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Optiver wasn’t unique in the industry for its policy of hiring young professionals, and the competition for talent is always fierce among prop shops. Also, these days, the industry is becoming much more high-profile and visible to job seekers, and many candidates do interviews at multiple prop trading shops during their job hunt.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Everyone is chasing the same top talent against competition from outside the financial sector, too. It used to be Big Tech companies that Optiver had an edge over, with its less bureaucratic, more cash-rich compensation structure. But these days, the strongest rivals for talent are AI labs.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Onboarding feedback loop</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>New hires enter a structured program called the ‘Global Optiver Academy,’ covering the fundamentals of business and finance, in addition to standard technical onboarding. After formal training, new hires join their team and get mentors who help them push their first changes to production within a few weeks.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The onboarding process itself is pretty standard in tech, but what’s interesting is that Optiver built a feedback loop between onboarding and hiring, with analytics teams analyzing onboarding cohorts. This is used to tweak hiring guidelines and interviewer training.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>9. Takeaways</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Here are the main takeaways we’ve taken after talking with the Optiver team, split as observations from the three of us working with the Optiver team (Ivan, Jesse and Gergely:)</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>The impact of optimizing for low latency</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>From Ivan Klaric:</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As an engineer, it’s interesting that latency optimization leads to the progression from high-performance C++ apps to custom chips. I love the “method in the madness” vibe.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Narrative-wise, a major detail is that everyone at Optiver is a trader, doing whatever necessary to make profitable trades. This drives the low-ceremony, extreme ownership culture, which in turn creates interesting tech stories like Linux kernel tweaks, custom networking equipment, FPGAs, ASICs, etc; basically, whatever it takes to make the best trade quicker than competitors.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The incentives are interesting. The nature of the business strongly incentivizes the heavy investment in testing, monitoring, and risk tooling. The business offers big bonuses which in turn drive extreme ownership culture, which can be both a curse and a blessing: it makes the leap into an AI-native world with collapsed roles a more natural progression, but the incentives can cause people to push back against the change.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>A different software engineering role inside of Optiver</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>Jesse Spevack shares:</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>AI means engineers are not the only ones writing code at Optiver today. Traders, researchers, and software engineers used to have stricter boundaries between roles, but Optiver’s researchers and traders have math and science backgrounds, while Cursor and Claude Code make producing code cheap. So, they can pair their domain knowledge and skills with AI.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>That doesn’t mean Optiver no longer needs software engineers. More of the team can produce code and trading strategies, but one mistake could still bankrupt the company. The tricky part is verification; perhaps Optiver’s platform engineers, on top of managing the company’s extreme latency and performance demands, will have even more work to do on validation, safety and risk systems. This work on validation, safety and risk systems keeps Optiver at the forefront of the prop trading industry.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Optiver controls its whole stack, from the integrated circuit layer up through network fiber and on-prem servers, to a global platform that enables all its market activity. The trading strategies come from researchers and traders with deep math and machine learning expertise, with a decade of “hill-climbing” on latency, from kernel bypass to custom ASICs. All of this is a moat that would surely take a tremendous amount of capital to compete with.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Similarities and differences vs “regular” tech companies and startups</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>Finally, from me (Gergely):</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>One of the biggest differences Optiver has compared to most tech companies is how it has no external customers. This creates very different dynamics: there are no deadlines from things that external customers would expect, but at the same time, there’s ongoing feedback about how much profit each trade and software feature made.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>With such a different set of constraints, it was interesting for me to look at what is similar in engineering approaches, compared to tech companies with external customers (like B2C or B2B tech companies):</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Design reviews are important. </span></strong><span>Bugs and mistakes cost money, so Optiver does reviews early on in the planning process to make sure they build the right thing, and get input to catch possible issues. This is similar to how today even leading AI companies like Anthropic do product review documents (PRDs) for complex, high-impact projects, as we covered </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/037b4f87-2e5c-4621-bf5c-63df80c8be3c?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>in our Anthropic deepdive.</span></a></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>CI/CD remains in-place. </span></strong><span>Verifying that software runs correctly is done with continuous integration and continuous deployment, and all the tests that run through these</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Small teams across the business. </span></strong><span>Teams are small across the org, at 5-10 engineers, even inside areas like hardware engineering.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>And some of the major differences to how SaaS tech businesses, and many startups operate:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Full control of hardware </span></strong><em><strong><span>and</span></strong></em><strong><span> software. </span></strong><span>Engineers at Optiver work on optimizations at the kernel level, and produce custom hardware to further reduce latency across their system. It’s rare for tech companies to get into producing custom hardware for their own, internal usage!</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Formal training after onboarding. </span></strong><span>Most tech companies and startups throw new hires into the deep water. Optiver, meanwhile, has a “Global Optiver Academy” teaching the fundamentals of business and finance to new joiners. I assume this is because many new engineer hires will not be up to speed with these topics: but they’ll need it to succeed at the company!</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Dealing with risk is part of decision making, across the company. </span></strong><span>Optiver – and other trading firms – are far more aware of the financial damage software bugs can cause, thanks to the cautionary tale of Knight Capital being destroyed with a single bad deploy. So while the lack of external customers would theoretically allow Optiver to move as fast as they please, wanting to minimize the risk of deployments means that they put in guardrails and checks to avoid software issues causing expensive incidents.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><span>I hope you enjoyed this deepdive into a niche, but exciting industry. Thanks very much to Alex Itkin, Pat Cooney, David Gross and the Optiver team for their time and input!</span></p></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;margin-bottom: 16px;overflow-wrap: anywhere;word-break: break-word;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em>This post is only for paying subscribers of </em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9uZXdzbGV0dGVyLnByYWdtYXRpY2VuZ2luZWVyLmNvbT91dG1fY2FtcGFpZ249ZW1haWwtaG9tZSZyPTM2eGwxbyIsInAiOjIwOTkzNDkzMiwicyI6NDU4NzA5LCJmIjpmYWxzZSwidSI6MTkzMDQzMTQ4LCJpYXQiOjE3ODY0NjU1MzMsImV4cCI6MjEwMjA0MTUzMywiaXNzIjoicHViLTAiLCJzdWIiOiJsaW5rLXJlZGlyZWN0In0.-N6-z35S8-BySv0x_oIesR6cOMpk59gzssEeaMDdHz8?" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">The Pragmatic Engineer</a><em>. 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For most of the web’s history, the question rarely came up, because the visitor was a person whose attention a site could sell through an ad or a subscription. If the website had good content, the website owner could count on multiple such visits by the same user. But now the visitor being a person is not always true. More than half of the traffic online now comes from software that acts on a person’s behalf, requests a page, and leaves without engaging with any ads or subscriptions [2].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Cloudflare seeks to change this.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As you might be aware, Cloudflare sits between a large share of the world’s websites and everything requesting them. It works as a reverse proxy that each request passes through before it reaches the origin server [1]. This lets Cloudflare read a request and act on it early. Over the past year, the company has used this position to sort automated traffic by what it does, to verify the identity behind a request, and, most recently, to collect payment for a request through an open protocol named x402 [1].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this article, we will go through Cloudflare’s solution in the following five steps:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The web’s usual way of earning value leans on human attention, and agent traffic changes it fundamentally.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: References at the end. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.</span></em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>The Attention Model</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For most of its history, websites made money after a request rather than during it. A browser asked for a page, and the server returned it at no charge. The value arrived later, once a person saw an advertisement, bought a subscription, or came back for another visit [1]. The request itself stayed free, and this setup funded a large part of the Internet.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A growth in agent traffic is changing this dramatically. An agent is software that acts on a person’s behalf, which in practice means it requests a page or a data feed once, takes what it needs, and finishes in a single pass. It moves past advertisements, operates outside any subscription, and completes its task before a site has a chance to earn from that attention [1]. Each of the three old settlement points depended on a person staying long enough to be counted, so software traffic leaves those points idle.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The strain here is that this kind of traffic is now fast becoming the majority. More than half of the requests reaching websites come from software rather than people [2]. This means that request volume climbs while revenue stays flat.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To make things clear, parts of the Internet were already charging by usage before any of this. Cloud services and APIs have been sold by the call and by the hour for years, though only to a buyer the seller already knew, who signed up and received an API key [1]. Charging an anonymous caller a fraction of a cent for a single request stayed impractical, because collecting such a small payment once cost more than the payment returned [1].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>If the value used to settle downstream of the request, the natural question is which party is positioned to move that settlement back onto the request. The answer starts with where Cloudflare sits.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>The Proxy Layer</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A reverse proxy is a server that stands in front of other servers and receives requests on their behalf. Since Cloudflare operates as a reverse proxy for a large portion of the web, a request headed for one of those sites reaches Cloudflare’s network first and passes through it on the way to the origin [1]. The origin is the site’s own server, the machine that ultimately holds the page or runs the API.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>On a side note, the position of a proxy is more general-purpose than caching. Caching stores a copy of a response so it can be served quickly the next time, and it is just one of the many useful things a proxy can do. From the same middle position, a request can also be read, classified, checked, and acted on before it continues to the origin. This broader capability is quite consequential at Cloudflare’s scale. [2].</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" a request early depends on first knowing what the request is for. This is a classification problem. Let us see how Cloudflare handles this.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Traffic Classification</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Before any rule can apply to an agent, the traffic has to be sorted by what it does. Cloudflare’s taxonomy groups automated traffic by behavior rather than by the single label “AI”. Three behaviors impact the key policy decisions [4].</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Search covers behavior that builds an index of a site so an engine can answer questions about it later. This behavior is responsible for sending referral visitors back.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>An agent covers behavior that acts in real time on a person’s behalf, usually with a human waiting for the result. Think of it like an assistant fetching a page during a conversation.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Training covers behavior that takes content to train or fine-tune a model, where the content is absorbed into the model rather than pointing a visitor back.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>These three appear identical in a raw request log, yet they carry very different consequences for a site’s business.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A single crawler can also perform more than one of these behaviors, but this separation lets them record all of them[4]. A crawler that both builds a search index and gathers training data is tracked as doing both, which lets a site owner reason about the full set of things that the crawler does on their pages.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Cloudflare classifies further behaviors as well, including checkout actions and data collection, and it also lets a site express what a bot may store and reshare after accessing a page [4].</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: the proxy position and a way to classify what arrives, let us now look at Cloudflare’s first attempts at implementing a policy.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Blocking and Charging</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Cloudflare’s first solution was a simple one. A single control lets a site block automated AI traffic outright. This protected the content and left the earning model untouched. Blocking answers the question of access, yet it does not rebuild the revenue that the old bargain provided.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The second solution added a middle path.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Pay Per Crawl lets a website allow a crawler, block it, or charge it a flat per-request price, with Cloudflare handling the billing as the merchant of record [5]. A site owner could keep a crawler out, let it through, or attach a price to its access, all from one setting. This turned the binary of block-or-allow into three options and gave content owners a way to earn from crawler access at network scale [5].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A year on, Cloudflare made an adjustment to its own model. The company argued that a crawl is a weak measure of value, because a single page might be crawled once and then cited in thousands of AI answers, or crawled repeatedly and cited in none [3]. It backed the argument with a figure from its own network, that more than half of the crawl traffic from well-behaved bots goes to re-fetching pages that have stayed the same since the last visit [3]. Counting crawls, then, counts something that only loosely tracks the value delivered.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>So the unit of payment began to move from the crawl toward the use, an approach Cloudflare describes as Pay Per Use. It is candidly framed as an experiment at this point [3]. This is because while pricing the outcome aligns payment with value more closely than pricing the fetch, it is also harder to measure.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>The Request Layer</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The design goal for recent changes is to resolve identity, permission, and payment inside a single request, at the edge, before the origin responds.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Three main concerns are considered over here:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Identity:</span></strong><span> The traditional identifier, the User-Agent string, can be set to any value by the caller, so it offers weak assurance. Cloudflare’s answer is Web Bot Auth, an authentication method that uses cryptographic signatures in HTTP messages to verify that a request comes from a particular automated source [7]. In practice, the operator signs its request with a private key and publishes the matching public key at a known location, and Cloudflare validates the signature at the edge [8]. A valid signature stands in for a reliable identity, which replaces a guess with a verifiable claim.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Permission:</span></strong><span> This is expressed through the behavior classification already covered and through the preferences a site sets about how its content may be used [4].</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Payment:</span></strong><span> This comes last and is attached to the request through x402. We will cover this in detail in the next section.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>All three concerns resolve at the edge, so the origin receives a request only once identity, permission, and payment have been settled [1]. The metering and settlement are taken away from the website’s own servers. What stays with the site owner is the part that matters to them, which is their rules, their prices, and their revenue [1].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To summarize:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Identity answers who is making the request, through a signed and verified claim.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Permission answers whether this behavior is allowed on these pages, through the classification and content preferences.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Payment answers whether the caller has paid the stated price through the x402 exchange.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>These pieces sit at different stages of maturity. Identity verification through Web Bot Auth is available today at the edge [7], while the Monetization Gateway that brings the payment piece together is open as a waitlist rather than a shipped product [1].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The key takeaway is that when one component sits in the middle of a flow, the concerns that are common across every request are collected at that point. Authentication, authorization, and billing consolidating at a gateway is the same pattern that appears in service meshes and middleware.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>The x402 Exchange</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The x402 protocol makes it possible to pay over HTTP. It takes its name from a status code that has been part of the HTTP standard for a long time [1]. The code is 402, and it means Payment Required. Sites behind Cloudflare already send more than a billion of these responses on an average day, which shows how often a machine requests something priced and receives a message that a payment is due [6].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>See the diagram below that shows the overall setup:</span></p><div through a short sequence that can be compared to a small state machine [1].</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A client requests a resource that sits behind a price.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Rather than returning the resource, the server responds with 402 and a small payload stating the price, the accepted asset, and where to pay.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The client re-sends the same request with proof of payment attached.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A facilitator verifies the payment, and the server returns the resource.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Two properties make this suitable for machine traffic. The payment amounts can be very small because the protocol adds almost no overhead to the request. And the payment itself serves as the credential, so a buyer with no prior relationship can access the content by showing the proof of payment [1]. This property is the one that matches an anonymous agent passing through once, since it removes the signup step that per-seat licensing and API keys always required.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The negotiation process is handled inside ordinary requests and responses, with a redirect to a checkout page absent and a separate payment API absent [1]. Nothing was added at the protocol level, since the 402 code has been part of HTTP for decades. What changed is that a settlement angle now exists that makes collecting a fraction of a cent practical.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Costs and Limits</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Resolving identity, permission, and payment at the edge means one proxy performs those functions for a large share of the web at once [1]. Cloudflare presents that responsibility as an advantage for settling everything inside one request. But it can also be seen as a potential risk when so much runs through a single provider.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Cloudflare also states several limits plainly:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Trust that travels with a request may reach only the traffic that can afford to be identifiable, and small or privacy-sensitive sources of traffic need other building blocks, such as private rate limiting [4].</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Usage-based payment helps a site that already has demand, and does little for a small site whose real difficulty is discoverability rather than monetization, which leaves that site weighing visibility against giving content away [4].</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Collecting a payment through this exchange depends on callers built to recognize and honor the 402 response. Therefore, the revenue depends on adoption within the ecosystem. [6].</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Pricing an outcome rather than a crawl aligns payment with value, but it is also harder to measure and verify. This is the reason Cloudflare frames the shift to Pay-Per-Use as an experiment [3].</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Lastly, Cloudflare argues that crawlers combining several purposes under one identity reduce transparency for a site. This is because the site cannot tell why it is being accessed [4]. While the argument is sound based on technical merits, it also aligns with Cloudflare’s commercial interest in separated, verifiable traffic.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>None of these costs undoes the shift. They simply mark the current trade-offs that website owners should consider before adopting it.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Conclusion</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The web is moving value settlement from after the request to inside it. For most of the web’s history, a request was served free, and value was settled later through human attention. However, agent traffic, which now comprises the majority of requests, leaves that later settlement with nowhere to land [2].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Cloudflare’s response is to resolve four things from its position as a reverse proxy: seeing what a request is through classification, verifying who sent it through Web Bot Auth, enforcing the site’s rules, and settling payment through the x402 exchange, all before the origin responds [1][4][7].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Identity verification lives at the edge today, and the payment gateway opens as a waitlist [1][7]. The open questions around concentration, reach, adoption, and how to price an outcome are worth tracking as the model develops.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: item.title: Relentless Forward Progress
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Relentless Forward Progress

Mike Fisher

“The hardest stretches of running a team are not sprints. They are ultras: the long downturn, the slow turnaround, the market that stays bad for six quarters straight. None is solved by a single heroic burst. They are survived, or not, by how you manage the long middle, when the adrenaline is gone and the only skill left is suffering productively while metering what you have.”_ _

#Leadership Management Wellbeing
item.description: Relentless Forward Progress

item.title: The Antithesis Principle
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
The Antithesis Principle

Shreyas Doshi

(1) If you want to help people learn something, look into making it engaging / entertaining. This first one is the easier, more obvious conclusion. (2) It is actually not in your best interest to be the kind of person who can only learn from entertaining content. Nor to be the kind of person that needs any sort of entertainment as a prerequisite for learning. The vast majority of smart people will never consider this second conclusion.

#CareerGrowth
item.description: The Antithesis Principle

item.title: Middle Management Roles Are Also A Trap
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Middle Management Roles Are Also A Trap

Will Larson

“If you’re willing to embrace this fact that a little bit of time in middle management roles is important preparation to become an executive, but spending a great deal of time in middle management only prepares you for further middle management roles–and makes you less effective as a potential executive–then the AI-driven shift in managerial fads might be a threat to your current role, but it’s likely to improve your chances to succeed as an executive.”

#Management CareerGrowth
item.description: Middle Management Roles Are Also A Trap

item.title: A Practical Guide To Rapid Onboarding
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
A Practical Guide To Rapid Onboarding

Steve Huynh

“After nearly two decades at Amazon, operating as a Principal Engineer, often parachuting into complex, high stakes projects, I’ve developed a system to cut through this chaos. In this article, I’ll share with you that exact framework to help you get up to speed unbelievably fast.”

#Management Guide Onboarding
item.description: A Practical Guide To Rapid Onboarding

item.title: Growing As An Engineer In A World Of AI
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Growing As An Engineer In A World Of AI

Norberto Lopes

“There’s a lot of buzz that AI means companies only want seniors now. That there’s no room left for early career engineers. I don’t think that’s true. The thing actually worth worrying about isn’t whether you’ll get hired, it’s whether you keep learning in a world of AI, now that it removes the friction where that learning used to happen. And that, thankfully, is a choice you get to make.”

#AI CareerGrowth
item.description: Growing As An Engineer In A World Of AI

item.title: Agentic Code Quality
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Agentic Code Quality

Addy Osmani

“For much of human history, we’ve evaluated code quality via code review: someone reads what you wrote and makes sure it’s clean, thoughtful, fast, understandable, and tests well. For agents, that approach doesn’t scale well; there’s just too much code for anyone to read. As a result, more and more of our quality checks have to happen in the harness, environment, and operating system around the agent. Software quality now depends on the constraints you set around your agents.”

#AI CodeQuality Agents
item.description: Agentic Code Quality

item.title: Beyond Happy Path Engineering: Databases
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Beyond Happy Path Engineering: Databases

Gabor Koos

“This series is about making your programs more resilient. Each post looks at one part of the system we take for granted: networks, time, databases, storage, users, dependencies, deployments, queues, and concurrency. The question is always the same: what assumptions are we making here, and what should we do when they stop being true?”

#Databases DeepDive
item.description: Beyond Happy Path Engineering: Databases

However, the problem is much deeper. It often sits inside the component that decides which posts become part of a user’s feed in the first place.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Consider the scale of the decision. When you open a feed, the platform has a few hundred milliseconds to select a handful of posts from hundreds of millions of candidates. Scoring every candidate with an expensive model burns through the time budget. To get over this, the social media platforms rely on engagement, which is a cheap and somewhat reliable proxy for judging relevance. Such a proxy is easy to measure and optimize against, and it powered a generation of recommendation systems.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" data-component-name="Image2ToDOMStatic" href="https://substack.com/redirect/3cdf0803-0923-4d66-ba47-9df9d424fd2f?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="position: relative;flex-direction:
