problem is that this type of engagement is also easy to manufacture. For example, a post that opens with “comment DONE if you’re a real engineer” collects clicks and replies while delivering little value. But a ranking function tuned to reward interaction will promote it even though it is clearly an engagement bait. For years, the countermeasures against this were heuristics and demotions applied after ranking, but such an approach hasn’t eliminated the problem. Accounts producing bait always find ways around such measures.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Over the past two years, LinkedIn, Meta, and YouTube, three of the largest platforms, have tried to address the root of the problem. All of them have attempted to rebuild the retrieval stage around the meaning of content, matching posts to people by what a post is about and how it relates to a reader’s interests. The idea is that once the relevance depends on semantic meaning, the tactics built for engagement farming lose their potency. However, the three companies have taken three different directions to solve the same problem, which provides us with an opportunity to understand things from multiple perspectives.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this article, we will work through the following points:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Why feeds relied on engagement signals for so long, and where that approach reached its limits.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>How embeddings match users and content by meaning.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>LinkedIn’s consolidation of five retrieval systems into a single language-model retriever.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Meta’s opposite choice of keeping a large family of specialized models arranged as a funnel.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>YouTube’s generative approach, where the system produces the identifier of the next item.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The cold-start problem, and why pretraining helps most when a user’s history is thin.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The tradeoffs each design carries, and the limits of the engagement-bait result.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><em><span>Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared details from various sources. References at the end. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.</span></em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Engagement Signals</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Every large feed runs on a two-step pipeline:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Retrieval: </span></strong><span>This step reduces hundreds of millions of candidates down to roughly a thousand. It has to be cheap because it touches the entire corpus.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><strong><span>Ranking: </span></strong><span>This step spends real compute ordering those survivors into the sequence you scroll.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Most of the recent architectural changes sit in retrieval, so that is where we will focus more.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For years, retrieval relied on behavioral signals. The system recorded which posts a user clicked, watched, and reacted to, then retrieved content that resembled those interactions or resembled the behavior of similar users. This approach scales well and produces reasonable feeds.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>However, it also has a weakness.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>When a system optimizes a single measurable objective, it tends to optimize the literal metric rather than the intent behind it. As mentioned, engagement is a proxy for relevance, and a proxy can be optimized directly. A retrieval stage tuned on interaction counts will surface whatever maximizes interaction counts, and engagement bait is the content that does exactly that. For example, content designed to trigger a click or a reply scores highly on the measured signal while contributing little to the experience the platform aims to deliver.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Suppressing such content through demotions and rules tries to treat the symptom without fixing the underlying disease. The retrieval stage still keeps bringing up the same material. A more durable fix changes what retrieval measures in the first place, and this happens by moving from behavior to meaning.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Semantic Retrieval</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The alternative is to retrieve content by its semantic content rather than by its interaction history. The ability to make this possibility depends on embeddings.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>An embedding is a list of numbers that positions an item as a point in a high-dimensional space, arranged so that related items land near one another. For example, a post about fixing a leaking tap and a post about reducing water waste sit close together even when they share no keywords, because their meanings are related. In more technical terms, the embedding reflects the relationship captured during model training.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To use embeddings for retrieval, platforms apply a dual-encoder design, sometimes called a two-tower model.</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>One encoder converts a user, along with their profile and recent activity, into a point in the space.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A second encoder converts each post into a point in the same space.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Since the two encoders operate independently, a platform can compute every post embedding in advance and store it in an index. At request time, it computes the user embedding and runs a nearest-neighbor search to find the closest posts, which keeps retrieval fast across an enormous corpus.</span></p><div design comes from what the embeddings encode. A keyword system matches surface tokens, so it links “electrical engineering” to other posts containing those words. An embedding produced by a language model reflects associations present in its training data, which lets it link an “electrical engineer” to other concepts like grid optimization and renewable energy infrastructure, even when the exact terms differ.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This same pattern appears well beyond social feeds. Search ranking, retrieval-augmented generation, and product recommendation all use two-tower retrieval. The model here transfers to a wide range of systems a developer might build.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>LinkedIn, Meta, and YouTube all adopt semantic retrieval, but they diverge in how they have built their respective solutions. Let us look at them in more detail.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Unified Retrieval</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>LinkedIn’s feed previously drew candidates from separate retrieval systems, each with its own index and its own optimization logic [1].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>One source supplied a chronological view of network activity, another handled trending posts by geography, another ran collaborative filtering, and several more produced embedding-based candidates. The setup worked, but maintaining five parallel systems led to rising engineering costs. Also, the sources were optimized independently rather than toward a single coherent objective.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In March 2026, LinkedIn replaced those systems with a single retrieval model built on a fine-tuned version of Meta’s LLaMA-3 [1]. The model acts as a dual encoder, converting both members and posts into one shared embedding space. It serves the entire feed through nearest-neighbor search at sub-50-millisecond latency for its member base [1].</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: model processes text, while a recommendation system runs on structured features such as view counts, engagement rates, work history, and post metadata. LinkedIn bridged this with a prompt library that converts structured fields into templated text sequences the model can process [1]. See the diagram below:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table member becomes a passage describing their profile, skills, and an ordered sequence of recently engaged posts, and a post becomes a passage describing its author, text, and engagement statistics.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We can also take a more general idea from LinkedIn’s approach. When the team fed raw popularity counts directly into the prompts, the numbers had almost no correlation with the model’s relevance scores, because large integers entered the model as arbitrary tokens. Converting each count into a ranked bucket, expressed as a percentage that the model could process in context, raised the correlation sharply and improved retrieval accuracy by roughly fifteen percent [1].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The takeaway from this is that the model is often the part that works, and the surrounding representation of the data is where the real effort goes.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>As we can see, consolidation is one answer to solve the retrieval question. However, Meta made a different choice.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Ranking Funnels</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Meta arranges Instagram’s recommendation system as a multi-stage funnel, consisting of an ecosystem of more than a thousand models supporting it [3]. Candidates pass through a sequence of stages, and each stage applies a more expensive model to a smaller set of surviving candidates [2].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The funnel runs through four steps:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Retrieval gathers candidates from many sources across the platform.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Early-stage ranking uses a lightweight two-tower model to narrow that set.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Late-stage ranking applies a heavier model to the remaining finalists.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A final pass adjusts the result for diversity and integrity.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Where LinkedIn moved toward meaning by consolidating, Meta pursues it through specialization.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In Meta’s approach, the late-stage model predicts many possible user actions at once, and a value model combines those predictions into a single score [4]. That combination adds weight for positive actions, such as a likely save, and subtracts weight for predicted negative actions, such as a “See Fewer Posts Like This” tap [4].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The basic objective of this extends past raw engagement to include signals about content a user would prefer to avoid.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" one many production recommenders resemble, which makes it a useful reference point. Many competing objectives, including engagement, diversity, integrity, and creator fairness, are easier to tune and audit as separate stages than as one model. Of course, the cost to this is operational complexity, which is the exact complexity LinkedIn set out to reduce.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>To summarize, both companies looked at semantic retrieval and made opposite conclusions about how much to consolidate. However, YouTube, the third platform we are looking at, questioned whether retrieval needs to search a stored index at all.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Generative Retrieval</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>YouTube took a third route that removes the search index from retrieval altogether [5].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The system, called PLUM, assigns every video a Semantic ID, a short sequence of discrete codes derived from the video’s own content [5]. Videos with similar content receive similar codes, so the identifier carries information about the item rather than acting as a random label.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>PLUM then adapts a pretrained language model (from the Gemini family) by adding these Semantic IDs to its vocabulary and continuing to train it on video metadata and user activity [5]. After this adaptation, the model performs retrieval as a generation task. Given a user’s recent history, it produces the Semantic IDs of the videos that the user is likely to watch next, decoding several candidate identifiers through beam search, and the system maps each identifier back to a real video [5].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>See the diagram below:</span></p><div however, introduces a failure mode that the index-based designs avoid, which is generating an identifier that maps to no video, and PLUM reports keeping that rate below five percent after fine-tuning [5].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The payoff from this solution appears in coverage. Measured against the previous production system, PLUM surfaced a far wider range of long-tail videos, and on YouTube Shorts, it raised panel click-through by 4.96 percent [5]. The architecture also inverts where the parameters live. The prior system stored most of its parameters in large embedding tables, while PLUM holds most of its parameters in the network itself [5].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Ultimately, the three designs converge on one payoff in the cold-start problem.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Cold Start</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A recommendation system faces the cold-start problem whenever a user arrives with little or no history. Behavioral retrieval has little to work with in this situation, because it depends on past interactions to find similar content, so new users historically saw generic material until their activity accumulated enough signal.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Semantic retrieval changes this.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Since a language model carries associations from pretraining, it can infer plausible interests from a profile alone. A member who lists a role in electrical engineering can be matched to content on grid optimization and energy infrastructure before clicking anything, using associations the model acquired during training rather than signals from that member’s own activity [1].</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>See the diagram below:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" capability also comes with a limit.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>An inference drawn from a sparse profile can be wrong, and it can compress a person into a stereotype built from whatever their profile most resembles. The strength and the weakness have the same source, which is that the model fills gaps with prior associations. LinkedIn’s reported results fit this picture. The overall lift from the new system was modest, while the gains concentrated among new and low-connection members, which is exactly the group a meaning-based system can serve when behavioral history is sparse [1].</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Design Tradeoffs</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Every one of these designs has an associated cost and tradeoffs.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The first is consolidation against specialization. LinkedIn’s single model is simpler to maintain and aligns retrieval with ranking, while Meta’s many-model funnel gives independent control over each objective and provides natural redundancy. A single model also raises a more difficult rollback question, because five specialized systems offered five independent places to intervene when one of them regressed on a case such as trending content.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The second tradeoff is related to cost. Language-model embeddings capture richer associations than the lightweight methods they replaced. However, they consume more compute to produce and serve. As LinkedIn’s popularity-count finding showed, the model is rarely the bottleneck, and the load moves to the data pipeline, the feature representation, and the serving path.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The third tradeoff sits between the generative and index-based approaches. Generative retrieval composes items from compact codes and removes the large embedding table, at the cost of a failure mode where the model can produce an identifier for a video that does not exist. Index-based retrieval avoids that failure mode, but requires storage and maintenance of the index.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: reduces the leverage of bait rather than removing it, since a system can still be gamed by content engineered to match high-value topics. Also, these three designs are points of emphasis on shared scaffolding more than pure types. YouTube still ranks candidates in stages, LinkedIn’s retriever feeds a separate ranking model, and Meta continues to explore generative methods.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Conclusion</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Social media feeds are transforming retrieval approaches from behavioral engagement to semantic meaning. This helps reduce the leverage of engagement bait as a property of the architecture.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>However, the three largest platforms adopted the same underlying idea and built it in three ways.</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>LinkedIn consolidated five retrieval systems into a single language-model dual encoder and searches one shared embedding space.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Meta kept a large family of specialized models arranged as a staged funnel with a multi-objective value model.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>YouTube generates the identifier of the next item through an adapted language model and removes the retrieval index.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The reason these choices differ comes down to data.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A text-rich professional network, a multi-objective media platform, and a video service with an enormous item corpus each favor a different design, and each team optimized for the structure of their specific data.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>References:</span></strong></p><p style="margin: 0 0 item.title: Beyond happy path engineering: Time
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Beyond happy path engineering: Time

Gabor Koos

37 minutes by Gabor Koos Gabor explains why time is more complicated in production systems than it first appears. He distinguishes wall-clock, monotonic, logical, and business time, showing when each should be used. He also covers clock drift, expiration, scheduled jobs, time zones, competing updates, and reconciliation. The main lesson is to treat time as a design boundary and make its assumptions explicit.
item.description: Beyond happy path engineering: Time

item.title: How to create your own decentralized messenger protocol
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
How to create your own decentralized messenger protocol

Michał Karbowiak

15 minutes by Michał Karbowiak Michał guides on building a simple decentralized messaging protocol using federation. He covers server discovery, user identities, end-to-end encryption, public key exchange, message delivery, and server authentication. He shows how clients can encrypt messages while servers securely communicate and verify each other. The approach provides a practical foundation for building a simple, decentralized messenger without relying on a central server.
item.description: How to create your own decentralized messenger protocol

item.title: Notes on incidents
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Notes on incidents

Sean Goedecke

6 minutes by Sean Goedecke Most incidents resolve without any action, and rushing to fix things often makes them worse. The best first step is to do nothing, take a breath, and observe. Simple fixes like disabling a feature flag usually solve the problem, but only if you know the system well enough to act decisively. Fixing incidents earns goodwill, but it is not a reliable path to lasting influence.
item.description: Notes on incidents

item.title: Growing as an engineer in a world of AI
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Growing as an engineer in a world of AI

Norberto Lopes

18 minutes by Norberto Lopes Norberto argues that leaning on AI to generate code without understanding it stunts your growth as an engineer. The learning that used to happen through struggle, repetition, and debugging is exactly what AI removes. To grow, he suggests treating AI as a thinking partner rather than an answer machine: ask why, type code out instead of pasting it, read the foundational books, and stay close to the hard conversations AI cannot join.
item.description: Growing as an engineer in a world of AI

item.title: 90% of the t distribution
item.author: Programming Digest <jakub@programmingdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
90% of the t distribution

Kqr

3 minutes by Kqr Gosset found that using a normal distribution to calculate confidence intervals gives results that are too narrow, because it treats an estimated standard deviation as exact. He developed correction factors based on sample size to fix this. With just two data points, you can estimate a standard deviation by multiplying the difference between them by 1.3, which helps judge whether a result is truly unusual. And the most popular article from the last issue was:
item.description: 90% of the t distribution

item.title: .NET 11 performance edition
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
.NET 11 performance edition

Steven Giesel

Steven looks into several notable speed improvements that .NET 11 brings with its release. Enum comparisons are 7x faster with no memory allocations, timezone conversions are 2x faster, and GUID parsing is about 20% faster. LINQ Min and Max see big gains for smaller data types like bytes and shorts, though integers and longs show little change. Results vary by machine and setup.
item.description: .NET 11 performance edition

item.title: Multi-Tenant .NET: Shared database with schema separation
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Multi-Tenant .NET: Shared database with schema separation

Barret Blake

Barret explains how to build a multi-tenant .NET application using a shared database with a separate schema for each tenant. He shows how this approach improves data isolation while removing query filters and tenant IDs. He also discusses the key EF Core model cache issue, schema provisioning, migrations, and the trade-offs compared with other multi-tenant designs.
item.description: Multi-Tenant .NET: Shared database with schema separation

item.title: Understanding the fetch metadata HTTP headers
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Understanding the fetch metadata HTTP headers

Andrew Lock

In this post Andrew looks at the Fetch Metadata HTTP headers that have been part of browsers for several years now. He describes what each of the four headers means, when they're sent, and how you might consider using them.
item.description: Understanding the fetch metadata HTTP headers

item.title: Adding a clone method to a C# record
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
Adding a clone method to a C# record

Gérald Barré

C# records provide a simple way to copy objects using the with expression, but sample with { } may not be obvious to every API user. Records also prevent you from defining your own Clone method. Gérald points out that a clean alternative is an extension method that calls with { }, giving consumers a clear and discoverable Clone() API while keeping the record’s built-in behavior intact.
item.description: Adding a clone method to a C# record

item.title: How to optimize SQL queries
item.author: C# Digest <jakub@csharpdigest.net>
item.ns0:encoded:
How to optimize SQL queries

Anton Martyniuk

Slow SQL queries can hurt application performance, but many problems can be fixed with a few practical techniques. Anton covers 20 ways to optimize queries, including using indexes correctly, fetching less data, simplifying joins, improving pagination, and keeping transactions short. He explains why execution plans and fresh statistics matter. The key lesson: measure first, then optimize what actually causes the slowdown. And the most popular article from the last issue was:
item.description: How to optimize SQL queries

item.title: Before You Delegate, Ask Yourself These 6 Questions
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Before You Delegate, Ask Yourself These 6 Questions

Wes Kao

(1) What does this person know? What’s new for them? (2) Why are we doing this? (3) What do they need in order to do this task? (4) What does great look like? (5) What’s the timeline and priority level? (6) What’s most likely to go wrong? What can I do to prevent this from happening?

#Management Delegation Tips
item.description: Before You Delegate, Ask Yourself These 6 Questions

item.title: The Big Management Lie: Overpromising
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
The Big Management Lie: Overpromising

“When managers are under pressure, and especially when they’re under pressure to retain a high performer, overpromising is one of the most common tools to reach for. The industry is rife with promises that someone will get a promotion, a new role, a large bonus, 5 more days of vacation, or any number of goodies, large or small.”

#Management Retention DifficultConversations
item.description: The Big Management Lie: Overpromising

item.title: Yes You Can Measure Engineering
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Yes You Can Measure Engineering

Jade Rubick

“I’d like to share my favorite way of measuring the value delivery of engineering organizations. It’s something I’ve used at a lot of companies. I call it the ValueSum metric.”

#Management Metrics
item.description: Yes You Can Measure Engineering

item.title: Finding Calm In Life And Work
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Finding Calm In Life And Work

Yew Jin Lim

“In a meta study involving 177 studies and more than 22,000 people, researchers found that being anxious reliably predicts worse performance on various measures, including working memory, which is the part of your mind that does the processing, the reasoning, and the problem solving.”

#Productivity Wellbeing
item.description: Finding Calm In Life And Work

item.title: Beyond “Clean Code”: Why Your Comments Matter
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Beyond “Clean Code”: Why Your Comments Matter

Tom Moertel

“To the extent that your programming language lets you express these things naturally in your logic, you should do so. But don’t contort your logic to accommodate intent and “why” information that would be easier for your audience to understand in natural language.”

#Communication CodeQuality
item.description: Beyond “Clean Code”: Why Your Comments Matter

item.title: Building An Advanced Agentic Harness
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Building An Advanced Agentic Harness

Bruno Gonçalves

“In this post we upgrade every piece of our basic harness toward that production shape, without hiding any of the mechanics behind a framework. The guiding question for the whole exercise is a simple one: How do you turn a single LLM call into a reliable system that can plan, act, recover, and prove it did the right thing?”

#DeepDive AI Agents
item.description: Building An Advanced Agentic Harness

item.title: How To Write An Effective Software Design Document
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
How To Write An Effective Software Design Document

Michael Lynch

“I’ve written design docs as a developer at Google, Microsoft, and within my own companies. The specifics vary, but the underlying principles remain the same. A design doc should articulate the hard problems you’re solving and help your teammates give you feedback. Below, I share my approach to creating effective design docs and explain what belongs in a design doc and what does not.”

#KnowledgeManagement Guide
item.description: How To Write An Effective Software Design Document

it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>A write operation records a fact, such as a new order, a changed email address, or a deleted comment. On the other hand, a read operation answers a question, such as which orders were placed this week or what should appear on a profile page. A single database on modest hardware can handle both types of operations without much trouble, and a developer need not be bothered about which operation is more common in the application’s context.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>However, high traffic can change things. Let’s say a page starts to load slowly. A fix is identified, which is creating an index on the column being filtered. Now, several months later, the same page is slow again under higher load. This time the fix is a cache in front of the query. A year after that, the database saturates during peak hours. This time the fix is a read replica with reporting traffic routed to it. In principle, each fix works, but each one is needed at a different time and for a different reason.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Now, let’s assume that a user updates a profile, reloads the page, but still sees the previous value. The bug does not reproduce locally, and it disappears on its own before anyone can investigate its root cause. However, this behavior can be a direct consequence of some of the other fixes. This is because each of the previous fixes placed a copy of some data somewhere other than its source. But the copy is not updated in sync with the source update. In other words, a seemingly simple fix on the read path can impact how things appear to work on the write path.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this article, we will look at read path and write path operations and techniques in detail. Here’s what we will cover:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Why fast reads and correct writes require opposing data structures</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Precomputation and duplication, the single operation underneath every read optimization</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Two different definitions of consistency, and the bugs caused by treating them as one</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Indexes, denormalization, caching, read replicas, materialized views, purpose-built read stores, fan-out on write versus read, and CQRS</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 They need specialized hardware, they consume large amounts of memory, and they add cost and delay to every request they handle.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>These traits make them hard to deploy in places where resources are limited, such as a mobile device or a service that handles heavy traffic and needs fast and low-cost responses.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>There is also a second fact that sounds backward at first. A small model can sometimes match or beat a much larger model on a specific task, even when the small model learned everything it knows from the larger one. On an intuitive level, a model trained on another model’s output would seem to inherit a ceiling rather than break through it, yet the results are different. The method that makes this work is called knowledge distillation, and it has become a standard part of how production AI systems get built.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>In this article, we will walk through the idea from the ground up. 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Distillation</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Distillation trains a new, smaller model to copy the behavior of a larger one. The setup involves two models:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The first is a large, capable model called the teacher.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The second is a smaller model called the student, which is trained to reproduce the teacher’s outputs.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Once training finishes, the student runs on its own, and the teacher steps out of the picture.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>A common assumption is that the student is the teacher in compressed form. The reality, however, is different.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Compression methods such as quantization and pruning start with one model and reduce its footprint by storing its numbers at lower precision or removing parts that contribute little to the result. The model stays the same model, smaller and lighter.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Distillation, on the other hand, produces a genuinely separate model, with its own parameters and often a different design, whose goal during training is to behave like the teacher.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>One operation shrinks an existing model. The other trains a fresh one. The payoff is practical, since a small student can run inside a single service or on a phone, respond in less time, and cost far less for each request, and in some cases, it can run on the device itself without sending data elsewhere.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 justify"><span>This method is now standard practice. For example, Google’s Gemma models are built using distillation during training, drawing on a larger model in the Gemini family. The two ideas also work together in sequence. A model is often distilled first to produce a smaller capable model, then quantized to shrink that model further for a specific device.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Keeping the distinction clear matters because it affects how we understand further concepts. A compressed model carries a copy of the original inside it. A distilled model is a separate thing that was trained to act like the original, which is exactly why it can sometimes behave in ways the original would not.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>If the student only copies the teacher, why does copying work so well?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The answer is in what the teacher hands over.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Soft Labels</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Learning from a model’s output beats learning from raw data because the output carries more information than a plain answer.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Standard training data gives one answer per example. An image of a cat carries the label “cat,” and the model is rewarded for producing “cat” and penalized for anything else. A teacher model offers something richer. Instead of a single answer, its output is a set of probabilities across the options, such as cat at 0.70, dog at 0.25, and fox at 0.05. That full set of probabilities is called a soft label, in contrast to the single hard label found in ordinary data.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The extra numbers carry additional information. They show that the teacher’s output ranks dog as a plausible alternative and fox as a distant one, which says something about how the categories relate to each other. Researchers sometimes call this dark knowledge, meaning the structure hidden in a model’s confidence that a bare label leaves out.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" justify"><span>During training, the student works to match this distribution. It is scored on how far its own probabilities sit from the teacher’s, and training pushes it to close that gap. In other words, the student learns the teacher’s whole pattern of confidence rather than a single right answer, and that pattern is a stronger training signal than a one-word label.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>This is the core reason distillation works as well as it does. A single correct label discards the relationships between options, and soft labels keep them.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>An early result showed the practical payoff, since a student could reach good performance from far fewer examples when trained on soft targets, because each example now carried more than a single answer. The original 2015 work added a control called temperature for exactly this purpose, where a higher temperature spreads the probabilities out and exposes more of that fine structure for the student to learn.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>With the mechanism clear, the next question is how this gets done in practice, which has more than one answer.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Methods</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Distillation comes in three main forms, and they differ in what the student copies:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Output distillation:</span></strong><span> The student matches the teacher’s final outputs, including the soft labels described above. This is the original form from 2015 and the most direct one.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Feature distillation:</span></strong><span> The student matches the teacher’s internal representations, meaning the intermediate values a model computes while processing an input, before it settles on a final answer. The aim is a similar internal picture, not only a similar output. Google’s EmbeddingGemma is trained this way, learning to produce internal representations close to those of a larger Gemini model.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Synthetic data distillation: </span></strong><span>The teacher generates a dataset of examples, and the student is fine-tuned on that dataset the same way it would be trained on any ordinary data. Stanford’s Alpaca was an early case, fine-tuned on examples produced by an existing large model to improve how well it followed instructions.</span></p></li></ul><div justify"><span>The third form has become the most common approach in practice, and part of the reason comes down to access.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Many strong models are reachable only through an interface that returns text, with their internal values and probabilities kept private. When those internals are out of reach, generating data is the route that still works.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The three forms also differ in what they require. Output distillation needs the teacher’s probabilities, feature distillation needs access to its internal values, and synthetic data distillation needs only the text the teacher produces, which is why it travels the furthest across closed models.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>These methods can also be combined. A single training run might use a generated dataset alongside soft labels, and newer methods mix teacher and student generation during training.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>These methods are not only theoretical. The next section shows what they produce.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Results</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The results in practice are strong, with one important qualifier.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>A clear example came in early 2025 from a lab called DeepSeek. It used a large reasoning model to generate a set of training examples, then fine-tuned several existing smaller models on those examples. One result stood out.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>A 7-billion-parameter student scored higher than a 32-billion-parameter model on a competition mathematics benchmark, even though it was produced by plain fine-tuning on the larger model’s outputs. The released family of distilled models ran from 1.5 billion parameters up to 70 billion, and the smaller ones were compact enough to run on a single graphics card, which is part of why the release drew so much attention. The practical effect was that strong performance on these narrow tasks became something a small team could run locally and cheaply, rather than only through a large hosted model.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The qualifier matters as much as the headline.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>These wins tend to appear on narrow, well-defined tasks such as mathematics and code. On those tasks, a small distilled model can perform at a level its size would not suggest. Across broader measures of general knowledge, the same small models still trail the larger ones. For example, a model can become excellent at competition mathematics through distillation while remaining weaker at wide-ranging questions about the world. Therefore, a claim that a small model beats a large one is usually true in a specific, narrow sense.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: justify"><span>If the results are this good, the natural question is where the method falls short, which the next section takes on directly.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Limits</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Distillation has clear limits, and they matter when deciding whether it fits a given problem.</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>A ceiling effect from the teacher:</span></strong><span> A student trained on a teacher’s output tends to stay at or below the teacher’s level on the kind of data they saw. When the teacher produces a wrong answer, the student learns that wrong answer along with the right ones. The teacher’s quality sets the bar, which makes the choice of teacher one of the most consequential decisions in the process.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>A wider gap can hurt: </span></strong><span>A larger, stronger teacher does not always produce a better student. When the gap between teacher and student is very wide, transfer can degrade, because the student has too little capacity to absorb everything that a much larger model expresses. Research on this capacity gap has found that the strongest available teacher is sometimes a poor choice. A set of methods exists to bridge wide gaps by adding a middle step, where the teacher trains a mid-sized model and that model trains the small student, so each handoff spans a smaller distance.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Architecture can outweigh size:</span></strong><span> The design of the base model can matter more than its parameter count. In one study, a 32-billion-parameter student outperformed a 70-billion-parameter student on the same task, because the smaller one was built on a stronger base architecture. Size alone is a weak predictor of how well distillation will go.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>The teacher can pass on more than the task:</span></strong><span> In a 2025 study later published in Nature, a teacher model with a particular trait, a tendency to favor owls, was used to generate training data made up only of number sequences. A student trained on those numbers picked up the same preference for owls, even after the data was filtered to remove any visible trace of the trait. The same effect appeared with more serious behaviors, and it occurred only when the teacher and student shared the same base model. The takeaway is that distillation can carry across more than the task being taught, and that filtering the visible data is sometimes too coarse to stop it.</span></p></li></ul><div justify"><span>These limits set the boundaries, and within them, the method keeps advancing. The next section covers where it is heading.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Automation</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The newest direction in distillation reduces the manual effort by automating the whole process.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>In this setup, the large model runs the full loop on its own. It generates training data, fine-tunes the student, evaluates the student against a held-out set of examples it also generates, and repeats the cycle, adjusting what it produces until the student stops improving. The human role shrinks to defining the task and the success criteria at the start, with a final check on real data at the end.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" justify"><span>Recent work in 2026 applied this to a detection task and found that it worked well, with one finding worth keeping in mind.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The choice of teacher model had a large effect on the outcome. Different teachers, given the same loop and the same student, produced students of noticeably different quality. So automation removes manual effort while making the initial choice of teacher more consequential, since that choice now drives an entire self-running process rather than a single training pass.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The same loop also points toward less hand-built pipeline work over time, as more of the data generation and evaluation moves to the model itself. For a team, the appeal is building a small, task-specific model without assembling a large hand-labeled dataset first, since the teacher supplies both the training examples and the data used to score them.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;overflow-wrap: break-word;word-break: keep-all;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Conclusion</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Distillation is a method for training a small, deployable model to copy the behavior of a large, expensive one. It produces a separate model rather than a compressed version of the original, and that distinction explains most of how it behaves.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>It works because a model’s output carries more information than a plain label, in the form of soft labels that show a full pattern of confidence across the options.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>In practice, the most common form has the teacher generate a training set that the student learns from, and the results can be strong, though usually on narrow tasks.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The limits are real:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The teacher sets a ceiling,</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>A wider size gap can hurt rather than help,</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Architecture can outweigh size</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The process can carry across traits that were never intended.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Taken together, distillation tends to be a good fit when the task is well defined and a capable teacher is available, and a weaker fit when the goal is broad, open-ended capability.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><strong><span>References:</span></strong></p><ul rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Why does sending a model a 100K-word prompt cost so much more than sending it a short one, even when the model and the hardware stay the same?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>A key part of the answer lies in a block of working memory called the KV cache.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>This memory is built up while the model generates a response. It is separate from the knowledge stored in the model’s weights, and it holds the key and value vectors computed for every token of the input. The cache grows with every token, and in a long context, it can take up significant space on the GPU.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>For example,  for a 70-billion-parameter model at a context of 128,000 tokens, it comes to roughly 40 gigabytes, a serious amount of GPU memory that grows with every user you add.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table In this article, we will learn how LLMs use memory, how it gets expensive, and how to fix it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><em><span>Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared details from various sources. References at the end. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.</span></em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Recomputation</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Let us start with the work a model does to produce one token.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>To choose the next word, it runs an attention step, where the newest token compares itself against every token that came before it. This comparison uses two vectors for each earlier token, a key and a value, which are simply the numerical summaries the model computes for that token inside each layer. A model that rebuilt the key and value for every earlier token at every step would watch the work per token climb as the input grows. Such a repetition is pure waste, because those keys and values stay the same once a token has been processed.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The KV cache removes the waste by storing those key and value vectors the first time they are computed. On the next step, the model computes the key and value for only the new token and reads the rest straight from the cache.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" justify"><span>Overall, this is a great solution. However, caching fixes the speed problem while creating a new one. The cache now has to be read on every step, and this turns out to be the real source of increasing cost.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>One detail worth understanding here is that the cache holds vectors rather than the original text. It also explains out-of-memory errors that look puzzling when the model itself fits with room to spare.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Decoding</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>Generation of tokens runs in two phases, and they stress the hardware in different ways:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The first phase is prefill, where the model reads the entire input at once. It processes all of the input tokens in parallel and builds their key and value vectors into the cache in a single pass. Prefill keeps the GPU’s math units busy, so we call it compute-bound, meaning the limit is how fast the chip can do arithmetic.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>The second phase is decoding, where the model produces the output one token at a time. Each new token runs an attention step against the whole cache, which means the model reads every stored key and value out of GPU memory before it can emit the next token. It repeats that read for every token it produces. The limit here is how fast the cache can move from memory into the compute units, so we call decoding memory-bound.</span></p></li></ul><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" justify"><span>The expense of long-context generation comes less from holding the cache and more from sweeping through all of it on every single token.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>A larger cache means more data crossing the memory bus per token, which shows up directly as slower and costlier generation. It also explains why a request can run slowly even when it fits in memory comfortably.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>If the cost tracks how much of the cache we read each step, then the size of the cache is the next thing to understand clearly.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Scaling</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>The cache size is the product of a handful of numbers:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>A factor of two covers the key and the value.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Layers count because each layer keeps its own cache.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Key-value heads set how many sets each layer stores.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Head dimension is the size of each of those vectors.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Bytes per number is the space one stored value takes.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Tokens are the context length, with one entry each.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Batch size is the number of requests served at once.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><span>To summarize, the cache size equals 2 times layers times key-value heads times head dimension times bytes per number times tokens times batch size.</span></p><div
