Jarred told me:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Today, a person presses ‘merge’ but within a few months, I expect:</span></p></blockquote><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Automated reviewer LGTMs</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>→ another Claude with a fresh context window judges if it’s simple and low blast-radius</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>→ if it is: auto-merge!”</span></p></li></ul><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Test assumptions with each model generation</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Inside Anthropic, the team keeps testing their priors. Thariq gave an interesting example:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“The thing with agents is that you have to revisit any assumptions you have made because it can change with a new model generation. For that reason, we deleted 80% of the Claude Code system prompt recently because the model has gotten smarter.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Using HTML is another assumption we needed to re-examine.</span></strong><span> HTML is one of those things which Claude is a lot smarter at than many of us expected. I’ve started preferring HTML as an output format over Markdown, and see this being used by others on the Claude Code team.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>HTML can convey much richer information compared to markdown, HTML documents are easier to read and share.”</span></p></blockquote><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>4. Team-level changes</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>At Anthropic, there are also changes in how engineering teams operate, compared to pre-AI.</span></p><div class="paywall-jump" data-component-name="PaywallToDOM" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;display: none;"></div><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Design is less upfront & more continuous on product teams</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Katelyn:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“As an engineer, you used to be able to say, “here’s a perfect, beautiful design.” </span><strong><span>In some teams inside the Anthropic org, upfront planning is gone.</span></strong><span> There are parts of the Anthropic org where people have said things like “we don’t write PRDs” or “we don’t write technical design documents anymore.” Those teams go straight to prototypes.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It’s worth bearing in mind the differences between platform and product teams, and the maturity of products. The more platform-like and mature a product is, the more that the value of upfront planning rises.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Silos no longer a worry</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Katelyn confirmed that while the typical size of the platform teams has not changed much – they’re still 6-8 people – but now, they take on far more projects than in the past.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Pre-AI, if a team worked on more than one project at a time, members would complain about feeling siloed: cut off from what peers on the team were doing. But now, it’s common to find 3-8 parallel projects on a 6–8-person team.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Two engineers max on individual projects</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Katelyn:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“On an individual project, you often cannot have more than two people working on it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>This is because each engineer is already running several agents</span></strong><span>. And so as an engineer, you’re already fighting against your agents, which are stepping on each other’s toes on implementation. And in this setup, you just cannot have that many humans, who also come with all their agents! This is especially true when the human is doing more of the actual design of the system.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Katelyn has a point: before AI, it was also a recipe for disaster to have several tech leads on the same project!</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Internal teams iterate faster</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Pre-AI, teams went through the back-and-forth of iterating on an implementation using design documents. Now, for the Claude Managed Agents project, it took the form of the Claude Code team hacking around the implementation. Katelyn told me the whole process felt faster and easier than before AI tools.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>5. Still the same</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Here’s what I gathered from my four conversations with Anthropic insiders about what’s not changed in software engineering much since AI came along.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Two-pizza teams</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>On the Platform side, there are 6–8-person teams as there were before AI in platform organizations. Katelyn on why this hasn’t changed:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I still have teams whose job it is to own a piece of software, iterate on it, own oncall, and so on. While each of these humans are supercharged by AI, the size and shape of the team is still similar. We still have two-pizza teams.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Everybody on the team needs to have a deep understanding of the system. </span></strong><span> They need to understand where it’s going, then orchestrate their Claudes to build in that direction. But people still need to internalize how their system works. So, the system they work on cannot become so big that someone doesn’t understand it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But then, you also need enough people so that when someone is oncall, another is on vacation, and someone is sick, you still have redundancy and the team can continue to make progress.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>One thing I’ve heard from some people is “we have two humans and a bunch of agents.” </span></strong><span>I reply that this isn’t where we’re at: we still have teams with 6-8 people on average.”</span></p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Planning still important</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Both Katelyn and Jarred mentioned the importance of planning, but with different focuses:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For Managed Agents, the planning process was the most similar to how it was pre-AI, due to the complexity:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Infrastructure complexity: the platform itself is complex, with lots of parts that needed consideration</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>The number of people/teams involved: a lot of people and groups needed to be aligned: not just the Platform team, but other teams at Anthropic, and working with three different cloud providers.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>This takes time to get it right!</span></p></li></ul></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>For the Bun rewrite, Jarred started by spending three hours talking to Claude about how to map patterns from their Zig codebase closely to Rust</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For complex projects with many people or systems, planning still matters at Anthropic. Even for kicking off a “simpler” project like a migration, a few hours of intense preparation and planning is seen as worthwhile.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Also, let’s not forget that in the Bun rewrite, the planning part was greatly shortened by Jarred being the creator and de facto domain expert. Also, there were no other engineers, which further shortened the process.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>PRDs in some teams</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>PRDs are for when lots of people need to be coordinated, and the Claude Managed Agents project is a good case. PRDs inside Anthropic are Google Docs because the point of this document is for it to be debated, and for agreement reached about a complex project’s high-level goals and design approach.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Platform/product split & prototype/mature product split</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>There’s a big difference between building a product and building a system, as with upfront design being far more of a thing with systems than it ever is with products.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For products, there is maturity to consider. For example, Claude Code during infancy was more of a prototype. It then found product-market fit, and today it’s a mature product with millions of customers. Prototyping can be a great way to get a product off the ground. But the more mature it becomes, the more planning might be needed for things like a new feature that needs to integrate nicely with other parts of the product, or product-wide changes.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It was the same pre-AI; we covered how Uber introduced platform and product teams in 2014 in </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/6a1c3c48-9b31-4648-a7f9-ca0a5d1abaf2?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>The platform/program split at Uber</span></a><span>, </span><em><span>the first-ever Pragmatic Engineer article</span></em><span>.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Platform work challenging as ever</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Katelyn, again:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“There’s a bit of a different working culture between application development and platform development. For example, when we’re building new things into the platform, we deploy on all three clouds (AWS, GCP, Azure), and deploy in several regions. We’ll eventually start deploying internationally. It makes for a lot of complexity.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>We have specialized teams within the org and a specialist team in each layer.</span></strong><span> We have abstraction layers in place, so most people don’t have to think about the physical infrastructure. But even so, within my org, I have a team who understand what queue implementations on each of the different clouds look like. In some cases, we’re running bare metal, and in other cases we’re running managed services. We always have a team that understands every part of a layer, and then other teams don’t need to become so specialist in a given layer.”</span></p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Context switching still hard</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I asked if it’s now easier to ask an engineer on another team for help with your own work. I figured it should be when everyone uses AI, as it makes getting back in “the zone” easy after returning to your work from lending a hand. Katelyn didn’t see it like that:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Context switching, on one end, is easier, but it’s still very hard. In the past, it was a pretty big ask to go to an engineer doing deep work, to ask them to stop something to help you with feedback, or do some of your work. With AI, context switching is easier, but deep work has not gone away.”</span></p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Agreement on interfaces still matters in cross-team engineering work</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Reflecting on Claude Managed Agents, Katelyn told me it’s important to define the interfaces between the Platform team building Managed Agents and the Claude Code team using it, as per pre-AI. The difference is that it’s a bit easier to iterate with AI:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>“</span></strong><span>Back in the day, you’d have to come with a fully spec’d interface you wanted to use with the team you’re integrating with (for us, Claude Code). Now, we can do it a lot more fluidly: we could stand up a stub service that shadowed traffic to start with, and iron out the interfaces with the Claude Code team as we went. They did some hacking on it, gave feedback, we made changes to it – we were building out the service under the interface – to make it work.”</span></p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Coding/testing time split hasn’t changed</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Time spent coding vs on testing hasn’t changed all that much from before AI,</span><strong><span> </span></strong><span>according to Jarred:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“The AI writes pretty much all the code, but we have the AI write pretty much all the tests as well. Before AI, for production-ready software, we spent about the same time writing tests as we did on writing code. This is still the case with AI. You need to have a way to trust your code, and tests are probably the best way to.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What happens to the time created by not spending it on writing code and tests? Jarred says he doesn’t have more free time these days:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I now spend more time on making sure everything works and on doing a lot more stuff than before. There’s so much stuff in Bun that we would not have shipped [without time savings from AI]. For example, we have a Markdown parser and a YAML parser on Bun. I used to have a list of everything I’d like to do in Bun, and it’s pretty much all there!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The bottleneck used to be me or someone else spending a bunch of time writing code, then spending just as much time figuring out how to test it all and what test suite to build. But now, we can just mention Claude in Slack (using Claude Tag), it runs and gives us a PR to start with.”</span></p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Learn something new to make something great</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Thariq Shihipar is responsible for much of the educational content on Claude Code. He’s a software engineer who tinkers a lot and shares what he learned; for example, how he got </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/82aebf22-5a7f-45a6-bebc-8dadb6e2ab23?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>Fable to edit a launch video.</span></a><span> He also works with the Claude Code team and engineers outside Anthropic.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table class="image-wrapper" width="100%" border="0" cellspacing="0" cellpadding="0" style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>One thing Thariq doesn’t see changing in engineering is that it takes special effort to make something truly great. As he told me:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“</span><strong><span>When you’re looking at how to make something great, you usually need to learn something new.</span></strong><span> Say that you want to make a video game. People love vibe coding video games, but there’s so much to learn to make a really good game!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>For example, if you’re making a flying game controlling a plane, there’s so much depth to how the plane reacts to the left and right movement. If you know about the domain, then Claude can work with you on it. But in my observation, you need to expand your own knowledge to be able to work efficiently with it to get to an end result that feels “great.”</span></p></blockquote><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>6. Changing the “standout” software engineer archetype?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I asked both Katelyn and Jarred if and how the “standout” software engineer archetype has altered with the adoption of AI tools, and which traits make for a solid engineer, in their view.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Understand, understand, understand</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Jarred:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“It’s still really important to understand how everything works, end to end. Also, it’s important to not trust that because something was assumed to be true, that it still is true.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>A lot of programming is still like poking around and seeing what happens. </span></strong><span>So, have the mental model in your head and stay in charge. As a person, I am still deciding what to merge, and what I should work on. I’m still very nitpicky about </span><em><span>exactly</span></em><span> the way it should be done, and this comes from understanding. I think you can also just use AI to help you understand faster.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Katelyn said similar:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>“Understanding is table stakes for solid engineers.</span></strong><span> Make sure you understand not just what the LLM does, but also a layer underneath it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The problem with models is the context window is finite. Our research team is working extremely hard so the model can feel like it has almost infinite context and that it will make the right decisions and store them away in memory, then pull it back in, and keep the  context window as clean as it can. But, at the end of the day, the model’s context window is finite and nowhere close to what a human brain can store – so keep investing in developing your own mind while you work with agents. Understanding and learning with the model is a great way.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Katelyn stressed that as an engineer, it’s important to understand not just the current layer, but also the one below it. For example, if building a product that uses queues, understand the queue primitive or implementation you’re using.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Coordination skill also table stakes</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Katelyn:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Coordination and alignment remain very important skills for engineers. Even if it gets easier to coordinate groups of people with AI tools, it’s not going away!”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I will add my own observation: every engineer I’ve met at Anthropic was a good communicator and articulate in expressing their ideas. I suspect the company would not hire folks who lack fluency in this and debating ideas.</span></p><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Engineers designing software</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Katelyn:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“Engineers are the ones doing the design, and it will probably stay like this for some time. Even as the models get better at technical design and systems design, I cannot see the model replacing my engineers on large-scale distributed systems design.”</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Steering the model in the right direction is very important. </span></strong><span>One more reason for understanding what the model does – and the layer below it – is that the model will get things wrong, inevitably. When it does, you want to steer the model to get it right.”</span></p></blockquote><h3 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.375em * 1);"><span>Being “in the zone” has changed</span></h3><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Jarred was a standout programmer pre-AI, and has spent a lot of his time “locked in” on writing code. Now that AI writes most of his code, I asked if he still gets “in the zone.” He told me:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>“Being in the zone” as a developer is definitely different now. </span></strong><span>I still do things in serial order, sometimes. Not writing the code, but when you’re doing one project, there’s a lot going on and you see it coming together, step by step. As long as the feedback loops are quick enough, I find myself in a kind of “zone.” It’s admittedly different from the “coding” zone, but it’s really fun.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Another thing I like is that I can be away from my computer, and things are still happening. For example, I can be on a run and just check how the agent running in the background is doing.</span></p></blockquote><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>7. Will AI replace software engineering?</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In February 2025, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/dbbce8b7-7147-4e4e-9254-5ab1855d50f1?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>made an eye-catching prediction</span></a><span>, saying: “coding is going away first, then all of software engineering”. His comment:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I think coding is going away first, done by the AI models first. And the broader task of software engineering will take longer. Doing that end-to-end [AI replacing software engineering] is going to happen as well.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>But the elements of design, or making something that is useful to the user, or managing teams of AI models: those things may still be present. Even if you’re doing 5% of a task, that 5% gets super amplified”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I asked Katelyn, Jarred, and David Hershey for their takes: do they see software engineering “going away” and being “solved” by Claude? </span><strong><span>Interestingly, people who build software day-to-day are not worried about models taking over software engineering. </span></strong><span>Katelyn and Jarred are confident they have lots of work to do, and feel busier with software engineering than before!</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>They do lots of planning, coordination, verification, coming up with more effective ways to manage agents, and building novel software.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>David Hershey, who focuses heavily on customers, reckons the models will eventually take over software engineering:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“I have a very hard time believing that the models will eventually not take over this thing that we call software engineering. It’s going to get better than us at nearly all of it.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The model can already listen to customer feedback, and write the software to solve problems customers have. It’s hard to point to something it cannot do.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>I watched models become better software engineers than me, and I have a software engineering degree. I don’t claim to be a great software engineer, but I don’t see why it would stop at my level and not keep outdoing most software engineers.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Based on my small sample size, it seems that the more hands-on someone is in software engineering, the less they believe the models will take their jobs. Both Katelyn and Jarred stressed the importance of understanding everything about your system, how it works, and to keep going ever deeper in understanding it – especially with the help of AI!</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);"><span>Takeaways</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>It was an interesting day at Anthropic, with much food for thought afterwards about the ways that software engineering has changed and where it might be headed next. </span><em><span>Thanks very much to everyone there for welcoming me and sharing their time.</span></em></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>I suspect the way software engineering is done inside Anthropic will be how many “AI-native” startups will operate soon </span></strong><span>– if not already. Specifically:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Projects done by a maximum of two engineers, and a bunch of AI agents</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Design is more ongoing and less upfront</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>A lot more prototyping, with more detailed planning only for complex projects</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>… but things still take time, even with faster coding! AI has not magically solved how to build quality software that’s complex and does something customers want.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>The software engineering bar has shifted upward at Anthropic. </span></strong><span>Every engineer I talked with there is “standout” in more than one dimension:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Solid engineers pre-AI: these folks were very good engineers before the AI wave</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Push themselves every day: they experiment with new approaches with (or without!) AI, change workflows, and keep learning how to best employ the latest models in their work</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;"><span>Collaboration and coordination are key: they self-manage themselves, stakeholders, and teams when needed</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>High-profile labs in leading positions like Anthropic get to hire the “best of the best” software engineers, and one question is what this means for companies without the brand recognition and funding of an Anthropic. Perhaps this kind of setup only works when you can hire such standout engineers, and for companies without the ability to attract such standout folks, attempting to copy what Anthropic does could well result in disappointment, without similarly motivated and capable staff.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Today, Anthropic generates five times more revenue per employee than Big Tech.</span></strong><span> Anthropic is made up of somewhat over 3,500 people, and annual revenue run-rate </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/a2c9d953-e36d-436a-891e-a4d51e242d37?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;"><span>crossed</span></a><span> $47 billion this May. That’s roughly $13.5M in revenue per employee: at Meta it’s $2.7M/employee, Apple $2.6M, and at Google $2.2M. NVIDIA is the only major company that comes close with $6M/employee.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure generated. Source: </span><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/27a0ed50-8200-4234-84f1-402b8b3d5fe7?j=eyJ1IjoiMzZ4bDFvIn0.YQmyE28ZLdSE7AAsuvKXIbV3t_oMMHyypLc7Hwjh0tE" style="text-decoration: underline;"><span>TrueUp</span></a></em></figcaption></figure></div><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Revenue per employee is one dimension that validates Anthropic’s approach of using AI as much as possible in everything they do, including software engineering. Such revenue also allows them to keep hiring top talent with the biggest comp packages on the market.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>We should state the obvious, that Anthropic is in the business of selling AI models, so using AI heavily is obvious for them. But they also support a very large number of customers and enterprises with a surprisingly small team, and using AI more than most companies is clearly one way to operate with so many fewer employees.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><strong><span>Teams are remarkably unchanged, though. </span></strong><span>One familiar part of how Anthropic works is that a “team” is still a core building block of the engineering organization, and it’s made up of 6-8 engineers as it was before AI.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The replacement of the team with two people and dozens of agents is not happening at Anthropic because it would not promote sustainable operations. As Katelyn said about the team size:</span></p><blockquote style="border-left: 4px solid #FF6B00;margin: 20px 0;padding: 0;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);margin-left: 20px;line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>“One thing I’ve heard from some people is ‘we have two humans and a bunch of agents.’ I reply that this isn’t where we’re at: we still have teams with 6-8 people on average.”</span></p></blockquote><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-bottom: 0;"><span>I hope you found this look into how Anthropic works interesting. In a future article, I’ll share details from inside OpenAI following a visit to their offices, and we’ll have the chance to compare the two.</span></p></div></div><div class="container-border" style="margin: 32px 0 0;width: 100%;box-sizing: border-box;border-top: 1px solid #e6e6e6;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"></div><div class="typography" style="--image-offset-margin: -120px;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="postscript" style="margin: 32px 0;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;"><div class="body markup" dir="auto" style="text-align: initial;font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;width: 100%;word-break: break-word;margin-bottom: 16px;"><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;margin-top: 0;"><em>This post is only for paying subscribers of </em><a href="https://substack.com/redirect/2/eyJlIjoiaHR0cHM6Ly9uZXdzbGV0dGVyLnByYWdtYXRpY2VuZ2luZWVyLmNvbT91dG1fY2FtcGFpZ249ZW1haWwtaG9tZSZyPTM2eGwxbyIsInAiOjIwODg0ODk0MCwicyI6NDU4NzA5LCJmIjpmYWxzZSwidSI6MTkzMDQzMTQ4LCJpYXQiOjE3ODUyNTQxMTIsImV4cCI6MjEwMDgzMDExMiwiaXNzIjoicHViLTAiLCJzdWIiOiJsaW5rLXJlZGlyZWN0In0.htbomr3SZp3auYhYhbphFOvnGxHWVe7wdnhJngfkr1s?" style="color: rgb(54,55,55);text-decoration: underline;">The Pragmatic Engineer</a><em>. They were also accessing more or less the same research base. And yet, the architectures they shipped look quite different from each other.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>That divergence is one of the most interesting aspects of modern development using LLMs. Once we understand why each company landed where it did, we will have a mental model for thinking about how AI can be integrated into any production system.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Adding an LLM to an existing stack comes down to one question: how deeply should the LLM reach into the runtime?</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Ultimately, DoorDash, Instacart, and Uber Eats each answered that question differently, and the specific LLM each chose was secondary. The specific model each company picked was secondary. The infrastructure they already had in place is what determined the answer.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>In this article, we will walk through their differing solutions and try to make sense of their choices and understand the pattern behind them.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><em><span>Disclaimer: This post is based on publicly shared details from various sources. References are present at the end. Please comment if you notice any inaccuracies.</span></em></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>The Problem</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Type “something healthy for a rainy evening” into a food delivery app and watch what comes back. The result we get today is somewhere between useful and impressive. The same query five years ago might have returned a random jumble of items, because keyword search treats the words as a bag of tokens rather than as an intent, and the query offers little for keyword matching.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>This pattern repeats across several common failure modes in food search. For example:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Synonyms:</span></strong><span> “Soda” and “soft drink” describe the same product, but a keyword engine treats them as different tokens.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Typos:</span></strong><span> “Mozzarela” should retrieve mozzarella results, but the spelling mismatch breaks the lookup.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Shorthand:</span></strong><span> “Gf pizza” meaning gluten-free pizza requires the system to recognize an abbreviation as a synonym for the full phrase.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Language mix:</span></strong><span> The Spanish word “pan” means bread, while the English word “pan” means a cooking vessel, so a bilingual search bar has to disambiguate.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Word-sense ambiguity:</span></strong><span> “Apple” the fruit and “Apple” the company share the same spelling but mean different things, and the right answer depends on context.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Each one is a potential moment where the user’s intent and the catalog’s words fail to line up.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px restaurant platforms see an enormous number of unique queries. rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>DoorDash already had a knowledge graph for items and restaurants when LLMs became viable for production. The graph held structured attributes for every item, including dish type, dietary preference, cuisine, brand, and flavor.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Their approach was to use LLMs to enrich this graph offline by extracting attributes from SKU data, and to use LLMs at runtime only for parsing queries into chunks that could link back to the graph. Retrieval itself stayed keyword and graph-driven.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Consider the query “small no-milk vanilla ice cream.” The LLM segments it into three chunks.</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>“small” is a quantity attribute.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>“no-milk” is a dietary preference attribute that maps to the canonical label “dairy-free.”</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>“vanilla ice cream” splits further into a dish type (”ice cream”) and a flavor (”vanilla”).</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Each chunk is then linked to a specific field in the knowledge graph. The dietary preference becomes a hard filter, so only dairy-free items get retrieved. The flavor becomes a soft preference for ranking. The dish type narrows the candidate pool.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>See the diagram below:</span></p><div DoorDash’s approach is how they constrain the LLM’s outputs.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>They use retrieval-augmented generation as a guardrail rather than as a generator. For each query segment, an approximate nearest neighbor lookup retrieves the top 100 closest taxonomy concepts from the existing graph. The LLM is then prompted to pick from that list rather than invent labels. This is a clever inversion of the usual RAG pattern, where RAG typically injects context into a generator. Here, RAG defines the entire output space, so the system only ever produces concepts that the rest of the design already knows how to handle.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The measured impact is a roughly 30% lift in the trigger rate for popular dish carousels, all delivered through an architecture whose runtime stays mostly classical.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The takeaway is that DoorDash’s LLM lives mostly offline, mostly in batch, working on the periphery of the runtime.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Instacart</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>When Instacart’s engineers first investigated an off-the-shelf LLM to categorize the search query “protein,” the model returned chicken, tofu, beef, and other high-protein foods.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The answer is reasonable by any reading of the English language. The problem is that Instacart’s actual users, when they type “protein,” are looking for protein bars and protein powders. The model’s general world knowledge and the company’s specific user behavior were pulling in different directions, and this small failure points at the central problem Instacart had to solve.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The system they were replacing was complex.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Query category classification ran on a FastText model, query rewrites came from a separate engine that mined session behavior, and spell correction, query tagging, and aisle classification each ran as a separate model with its own data pipeline and serving infrastructure. The maintenance burden was substantial, and tail queries still suffered because each model needed its own labeled data, and labels for rare queries are scarce by definition.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Instacart’s strategy is layered across three approaches:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Context engineering:</span></strong><span> Retrieval-augmented generation pulls Instacart-specific context (top-converted categories, historical conversion data, catalog details) into the prompt before the LLM sees a query.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Post-processing guardrails:</span></strong><span> Semantic similarity filters drop LLM outputs that drift away from the original query.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><strong><span>Fine-tuning:</span></strong><span> For the most advanced tasks, the team fine-tunes Llama-3-8B on Instacart’s proprietary data, so domain knowledge gets baked directly into the model weights.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>See the diagram below:</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px architecture splits along the head-versus-tail distribution.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Head queries hit an offline RAG-and-cache pipeline that is latency-tolerant and deeply context-engineered, while tail queries hit a real-time fine-tuned Llama-3-8B model that keeps latency under 300ms through adapter merging, H100 GPUs, and autoscaling.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The cache serves queries the company has seen before, while the real-time fine-tuned model serves everything else, which is where the cold-start tail lives. This split is exactly the kind of decision the head-versus-tail traffic distribution encourages, since pre-computing only pays off for queries that repeat.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>After this solution, query rewrite coverage jumped from 50% to over 95%, with 90%+ precision across substitutes, broader rewrites, and synonyms. The real-time fine-tuned model improved search quality for the bottom 2% of queries (the cold-start tail), cutting scroll depth by 6% and complaints about poor tail-query results by half.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The takeaway is that Instacart’s LLMs live at the query understanding layer, with some offline-cached and some online and fine-tuned, while retrieval and ranking downstream are still done by traditional machine learning and information retrieval systems. The LLM brain is doing the upstream interpretation, while the classical approach is doing the downstream serving.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Uber Eats</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Uber Eats faced the same problem the others did, plus a complication. They run across multiple verticals, including restaurants, grocery, and retail, across multiple markets, and across a long list of languages.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Their previous setup was fragmented, with separate BERT-based embedding models per vertical, lexical search in places, and the operational overhead of maintaining all of these in parallel. The goal was a single retrieval system that handled every vertical, every market, and every language with one consistent embedding space.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The architecture they decided on is a classic two-tower setup, where a query encoder and a document encoder each produce vectors in a shared space, and matching is done by similarity in that space.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The twist is in what sits inside each tower, because both towers use a fine-tuned Qwen LLM as their backbone embedding layer. The query tower runs online, embedding each incoming query in real time, while the document tower runs offline and pre-embeds billions of documents into an HNSW vector index (a graph-based structure built for fast similarity search at scale). This split is what makes the system economically possible, since running a heavyweight LLM on every document at query time would be prohibitive, while pre-computing once and looking up at retrieval time is tractable.</span></p><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: 100%;margin: 0 auto;"><table matters as much as the architecture choice.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Out of the box, Qwen brings world knowledge and cross-lingual capability, which is what handles the Spanish “pan” problem mentioned earlier. Fine-tuning on Uber’s proprietary query-document interactions teaches the embedding space what Uber Eats users actually care about, and this is what gives the system its domain alignment. The base model contributes general semantics, and the fine-tuning adds the specific rules of Uber Eats.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>What makes the system viable at scale is a stack of optimizations:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Matryoshka Representation Learning trains a single model whose embedding can be truncated to different lengths, and Uber serves at 256 dimensions in production with under 0.3% recall loss compared to the full 1,536.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Scalar quantization (int7 instead of float32) cuts latency in half again.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Pre-filters on hexagon, city, and fulfillment type shrink the candidate set before the ANN search even runs.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The numbers tell the cost story. Tuning the ANN parameter k dropped latency by 34% and CPU by 17% with negligible recall impact, quantization halved latency at recall above 0.95, and MRL cut storage by nearly 50%. Together, these are the engineering choices that let a fine-tuned LLM serve as the retrieval substrate of a production search system at Uber Eats’ scale.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The takeaway is that Uber Eats’ LLM is the embedding model itself, since every query and every document gets an LLM-derived vector, and retrieval at every level depends on LLM-produced representations.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Integration Depth</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>If we line up the three companies on a single axis labeled “how deeply does the LLM sit in the runtime,” the pattern provides some insight.</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>DoorDash sits on the left, with the LLM enriching the catalog offline and parsing queries with constrained outputs while the runtime stays 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Uber Eats sits on the right, with a fine-tuned Qwen as the embedding backbone running for every query and pre-baked into every document vector.</span></p></li></ul><div class="captioned-image-container-static" style="font-size: 16px;line-height: 26px;margin: 32px auto;"><figure style="width: style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>DoorDash already had a knowledge graph that classical retrieval could exploit, so the cheapest gain came from making the graph richer and teaching queries how to talk to it.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Instacart had specialized query-understanding models that were hard to maintain, so the biggest win came from consolidation under a unified LLM strategy.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Uber Eats already had two-tower embedding infrastructure running per vertical, so the natural next step was swapping in a fine-tuned LLM as the shared backbone, allowing one model to handle every vertical and every language.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The lesson would be that before asking which LLM to use for some task, the better question is where in an existing stack an LLM would actually help.</span></p><h2 class="header-anchor-post" style="position: relative;font-family: 'SF Pro Display',-apple-system-headline,system-ui,-apple-system,BlinkMacSystemFont,'Segoe UI',Roboto,Helvetica,Arial,sans-serif,'Apple Color Emoji','Segoe UI Emoji','Segoe UI Symbol';font-weight: bold;-webkit-font-smoothing: antialiased;-moz-osx-font-smoothing: antialiased;-webkit-appearance: optimizelegibility;-moz-appearance: optimizelegibility;appearance: optimizelegibility;margin: 1em 0 0.625em 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 1.16em;font-size: calc(1.625em * 1);text-align: justify"><span>Conclusion</span></h2><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Three of the largest food delivery companies rebuilt search around LLMs in the same window of time, with overlapping research literature and similar production constraints, and they arrived at three completely distinct architectures.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The reason food search was a good place to investigate this is that it breaks classical keyword retrieval in many ways simultaneously. Subjective queries (something healthy for a rainy evening), long-tail traffic, multilingual catalogs, and compound constraints all sit in the same search bar.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>The three approaches each represent a different setting:</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>DoorDash uses LLMs offline to enrich a knowledge graph, while classical retrieval still drives the runtime.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Instacart uses LLMs at the query understanding layer, with fine-tuned smaller models handling tail queries in the hot path.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Uber Eats fine-tuned a Qwen LLM into the embedding backbone of two-tower retrieval, so every query and every document gets an LLM-derived vector.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Each company’s position on this spectrum traces back to the infrastructure it already had, which is why the depth-of-integration question matters more than the model choice.</span></p><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;"><span>Three universal tradeoffs survived every architecture.</span></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Hybrid systems are the default everywhere. Classical retrieval, knowledge graphs, and ANN indexes still do most of the work.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>World knowledge from a pre-trained model is just a head start. Domain context still has to be injected somewhere, through RAG, fine-tuning, or both.</span></p></li><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><span>Guardrails are an important part of every production LLM system. Constrained vocabularies, similarity filters, and taxonomy enforcement quietly determine whether outputs stay aligned with the catalog.</span></p></li></ul><p style="margin: 0 0 20px 0;color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;font-size: 16px;text-align: justify"><strong><span>References:</span></strong></p><ul style="margin-top: 0;padding: 0;"><li style="margin: 8px 0 0 32px;mso-special-format: bullet;"><p style="color: rgb(54,55,55);line-height: 26px;margin-bottom: 0;box-sizing: border-box;padding-left: 4px;font-size: 16px;margin: 0;text-align: justify"><a item.title: Mission To Metrics
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Mission To Metrics

Annie Zhou

“Mission to Metrics is a written cascade, running from why the org exists down to the numbers that measure whether it’s getting there. Every team’s plan is a more detailed version of one slice of the layer above. Every metric traces back to the mission. Once it’s written, anyone in the org can read the page and understand how their work connects to the company mission.”

#Leadership Management Metrics
item.description: Mission To Metrics

item.title: The Vital Few
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
The Vital Few

Mike Fisher

“Stewardship is the actual work. It means giving your strongest people air cover, not just assignments. It means defending their focus from the steady drizzle of interruptions that drifts toward competence. It means offering them growth rather than merely more volume, and fighting the reflex to drop the next critical thing on the proven desk simply because it is proven.”

#Leadership Management Retention
item.description: The Vital Few

item.title: Make No Assumptions
item.author: Pointer <suraj@pointer.io>
item.ns0:encoded:
Make No Assumptions

Will Larson

“When that architect leaves, they are replaced by someone who aspires to operate in the same code layer, but simply cannot because they lack enough context to do so. As a result, that new replacement creates a new code layer, despite not intending to. If the team runs through a handful of folks as the new team leads struggle, it’s easy to end up with a complex code horizon very quickly.”

#Leadership AI CodeReview
item.description: Make No Assumptions
